teile.einleitung: A minute is a unit of time and lasts exactly 60 seconds. Sixty minutes make an hour. We use minutes every day to read the clock, catch the bus or brush our teeth for long enough.
wichtigste: A minute has 60 seconds, and an hour has 60 minutes.
The symbol for minute is min.
A quarter of an hour has 15 minutes, three quarters of an hour have 45 minutes.
An hour and a half is 90 minutes.
A day has 1440 minutes.
You should brush your teeth for about 2 to 3 minutes.
Dividing into 60 comes from the ancient Babylonians.

abschnitte.text: The **minute** is a unit of time. It lasts exactly 60 **seconds**, and 60 minutes make an **hour**. So a whole day with 24 hours has 24 times 60, which is 1440 minutes. It is written in short as min, for example 5 min. The word comes from the Latin pars minuta prima, which means “first small part”.

On a clock with hands, the long hand shows the minutes. It takes one hour to go all the way round, and each small mark on the clock face stands for one minute. There are 5 minutes between two numbers. A **quarter of an hour** has 15 minutes, half an hour has 30 minutes. On a digital clock, the minutes come after the colon or, in Switzerland, often after a full stop, such as 10.50.

When you calculate with time, remember that a new hour begins after 59 minutes. For example, it is 10.50, and 20 minutes later it is 11.10, because 10 minutes are missing until the full hour and then another 10 are added. An hour and a half is 60 plus 30, so 90 minutes. A football match lasts two halves of 45 minutes, which is also 90 minutes. You need calculations like these when reading timetables, for example.

The fact that an hour has 60 minutes goes back to the **Babylonians** in ancient Mesopotamia. They used a number system based on the number 60, the **sexagesimal system**. The number 60 can be divided by many numbers: 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 10, 12, 15, 20 and 30. That is why an hour can easily be split into halves, thirds or quarters. However, clocks with minute hands only became common in the 17th century, when clocks became more accurate.

A famous example of the minute is the **Swiss railway clock**, which Hans Hilfiker designed for the SBB in 1944. Its red second hand with the round disc goes round a little faster than one minute. At the top, at the 12, it stops briefly until a signal arrives. Then the minute hand jumps forward one minute, and all the clocks in the country show the new minute at the same time. This way the trains leave on time to the minute.

The word minute is also used when measuring **angles**. A degree is divided into 60 minutes of arc, just like an hour. This is needed, for example, for coordinates on maps and at sea. The minute of time and the minute of arc have the same origin in the Babylonian number system. For angles, you write a small dash, for example 30 degrees and 15 minutes.

begriffe.erklaerung: The 60th part of a minute.
15 minutes, a quarter of an hour.
A number system based on the number 60.
The surface of a clock with the numbers and marks.

gewusst: Because of the leap second, a minute has already had 61 seconds several times.
A child's heart beats about 80 to 100 times in a minute.
The SBB railway clock is so well known that its design has also been used for wristwatches.

teile.einleitung: The eyepiece is the lens of a microscope or telescope that you look into with your eye. It works like a magnifying glass and enlarges the image formed by the objective. Without an eyepiece, you could hardly see anything through a telescope.
wichtigste: The eyepiece is the lens on the side of the eye.
Its German name, Okular, comes from the Latin word “oculus”, which means eye.
The eyepiece works like a magnifying glass for the intermediate image of the objective.
Around 1660, Christiaan Huygens developed an eyepiece made of two lenses.
A telescope's magnification is the focal length of the objective divided by the focal length of the eyepiece.
A telescope with a focal length of 1200 millimetres magnifies 120 times with a 10-millimetre eyepiece.
People who wear glasses need eyepieces with a long eye relief.

abschnitte.text: Telescopes and microscopes have two important lens systems. The **objective** points towards the object and forms a small image inside, the **intermediate image**. The **eyepiece** sits at the other end, right in front of the eye. It works like a magnifying glass with which you look at this intermediate image enlarged. Its German name, Okular, comes from the Latin “oculus”, which means eye.

For a telescope, the magnification is easy to work out. You divide the **focal length** of the objective by the focal length of the eyepiece. If a telescope has a focal length of 1200 millimetres and the eyepiece 10 millimetres, it magnifies 120 times. So an eyepiece with a short focal length magnifies more. That is why amateur astronomers often have several **interchangeable eyepieces** to choose between low and high magnification.

On a microscope, the eyepiece usually has a number on it such as 10x. You get the **total magnification** by multiplying this number by the magnification of the objective, for example 10 times 40 equals 400 times. Many microscopes have two eyepieces so that you can look in with both eyes. A **measuring eyepiece** has a built-in scale with which you can read off the size of cells or other things in the specimen. Microscopes like these are found in many Swiss schools.

The first telescopes were made in the Netherlands at the beginning of the 17th century. Galileo Galilei used a diverging lens as an eyepiece; Johannes Kepler suggested a converging lens. Around 1660, the Dutch physicist **Christiaan Huygens** developed an eyepiece made of two lenses, which is named after him. Later many other designs were added, such as the eyepiece by Jesse Ramsden. Modern eyepieces often consist of five or more lenses and give a large, sharp field of view.

If you wear glasses, you need an eyepiece with a long **eye relief** so that you can see the whole field of view despite your glasses. Some eyepieces have a rubber eyecup for this that you can fold down. On binoculars, one eyepiece lets you adjust the focus for each eye separately. You should never touch the glass surfaces with your fingers and should only clean them with a soft cloth. Important: never look at the **Sun** through a telescope without a special filter, as this can seriously injure your eye immediately.

begriffe.erklaerung: The lens of an optical instrument that you look through with your eye.
The image the objective forms inside the instrument.
A converging lens through which you see things enlarged.
How far your eye can be from the eyepiece and still see everything.

gewusst: With his telescopes, Christiaan Huygens also discovered Titan, the large moon of the planet Saturn.
If you magnify too much, the image gets bigger but also darker and blurrier.
On a microscope with a camera, a screen sometimes replaces the eyepiece completely.

teile.einleitung: The money of Switzerland is the Swiss franc, which is divided into 100 centimes (Rappen). There are seven coins and six different banknotes. The coins are minted by Swissmint in Bern, and the banknotes are issued by the Swiss National Bank.
wichtigste: The currency of Switzerland is the Swiss franc, abbreviated CHF.
One franc has 100 centimes (Rappen).
There are coins worth 5, 10 and 20 centimes and ½, 1, 2 and 5 francs.
The five-franc piece is the largest Swiss coin; the most drops of water fit on it.
The banknotes come in 10, 20, 50, 100, 200 and 1000 francs.
The coins are minted by Swissmint in Bern; the banknotes are issued by the Swiss National Bank.
The franc has been the common currency of the whole of Switzerland since 1850.

abschnitte.text: Switzerland has seven **coins**: 5, 10 and 20 centimes and ½, 1, 2 and 5 francs. The 5-centime piece is gold-coloured; the other coins are silvery. The centime coins show the head of the goddess of liberty, Libertas. The ½, 1 and 2-franc pieces show Helvetia, a female figure who represents Switzerland. The five-franc piece shows the head of an alpine herdsman and is popularly called the **Fünfliber**.

You can do an exciting experiment with coins: how many drops of water fit on a coin? Using a pipette, you carefully drip water onto it. The water bulges upwards like a dome before it overflows. The reason is **surface tension**: the water particles hold on to each other like a thin skin. The most drops fit on the five-franc piece, because it has the largest surface.

The banknotes come in 10, 20, 50, 100, 200 and 1000 francs. The current ninth series was introduced between 2016 and 2019. Each note has a theme that shows the many sides of Switzerland, for example time, light, wind, water, matter and communication. A hand and a globe can be found on all the notes. The 1000-franc note is one of the banknotes with the highest value in the world.

Banknotes have many **security features** so that they are hard to forge. These include a security thread, shiny elements that change colour when you tilt them, and raised printing you can feel. If you hold a note up to the light, you can see a Swiss cross. The coins also have features on the edge. The edge of the Fünfliber bears the inscription “Dominus providebit”, which means “The Lord will provide”.

The coins are made by **Swissmint**, the federal mint in Bern. The banknotes are issued by the **Swiss National Bank** and printed in Zurich. Before the Swiss franc existed in 1850, many cantons had their own money. That made paying complicated, because you constantly had to convert. The 1-centime coin was abolished in 2007 because it was hardly used any more.

begriffe.erklaerung: The hundredth part of a franc.
The everyday name for the five-franc piece.
The force with which water particles hold together at the surface.
The federal mint in Bern, which strikes the Swiss coins.
The state's bank, which issues the money and keeps the franc stable.

gewusst: Swiss coins have looked almost the same for over a hundred years.
The abbreviation CHF comes from “Confoederatio Helvetica” and franc.

teile.einleitung: A bed of nails is a board with a great many sharp nails sticking out of it close together. Amazingly, you can lie down on it without getting hurt. The bed of nails is a well-known example of how pressure depends on the size of the area.
wichtigste: On a bed of nails, the body's weight is spread over a great many points.
Pressure is force divided by area.
The more nails carry the weight, the smaller the force on each single nail.
All the nails must be exactly the same height, or a few nails carry the whole weight.
When standing, the pressure on the soles of the feet is greater than when lying down.
The bed of nails is known as a trick performed by fakirs.
The word fakir comes from Arabic and means “poor”.

abschnitte.titel: What is a bed of nails
abschnitte.text: A bed of nails is a wooden board with hundreds or even thousands of nails whose points face upwards. The nails are only a few centimetres apart and all the same length. Anyone who carefully lies down on it feels many small points but does not get hurt. It is often shown in shows, museums and physics lessons.

abschnitte.titel: Pressure is force divided by area
abschnitte.text: **Pressure** tells you how strongly a force presses on a certain area. It is calculated as force divided by area, and the unit is the **pascal**. If the area is small, the pressure becomes large; if it is large, the pressure becomes small. A single nail has a tiny point and so easily pierces the skin.

If a person with a weight of 600 newtons lies evenly on 600 nails, each nail carries only 1 newton. That is about the weight of a bar of chocolate. If 500 newtons are spread over 1000 points, each with an area of 1 mm², the pressure is **500,000 pascals**. That is not enough to pierce the skin, but a single nail carrying the whole weight would go in deep.

On a board with only a few nails, each nail would have to carry much more weight, which would be dangerous. The height must be right too: if one nail sticks out further, it carries a large part of the load on its own. If you stand on the board instead of lying, the whole weight rests on the small soles of your feet and the pressure becomes greater. That is why you should never try such experiments without guidance from experts.

Lying on beds of nails is often linked with **fakirs**. The word comes from the Arabic word for “poor” and originally meant religious begging monks. In India, some ascetics showed how they could bear pain. Later, the bed of nails became a popular trick in the circus and at fairs.

abschnitte.titel: The same principle in everyday life
abschnitte.text: Stepping barefoot on a small toy brick hurts a lot, because the whole weight presses on a tiny area. **Snowshoes**, on the other hand, spread the weight over a large area so that you do not sink into the snow. Wide tyres on tractors protect the ground for the same reason. Knives and needles work the other way round: their fine edge or point creates enormous pressure.

begriffe.erklaerung: Force acting on a certain area.
The unit of pressure, one newton per square metre.
Originally a poor, religious begging monk; today also a performer who lies on nails.
The force with which the Earth pulls an object downwards.

gewusst: Because the weight is spread over many points, usually only small red dots are left on the skin after getting up.
A bed with only a few nails is more dangerous than one with many nails.
There are mats with many small plastic spikes that people lie on to relax.

teile.einleitung: A multimeter is a measuring device that can measure several electrical quantities. You use it to check voltage, current and resistance. Electricians, hobbyists and physics classes use it every day.
wichtigste: A multimeter measures several electrical quantities, mainly voltage, current and resistance.
The black test lead usually goes into the COM socket.
A straight line next to the symbol stands for direct current, a wavy line for alternating current.
If you do not know how big a value is, you first choose the largest measuring range.
Resistance is only measured with the circuit switched off, because the device itself produces a measuring current.
A minus sign for direct voltage shows that the leads are swapped.
For large currents, you put the red lead into the 10A socket.
In a continuity test, the device beeps if a wire is connected all the way through.

abschnitte.text: The word **multimeter** means something like multiple meter. In the past, you needed a separate device each for voltage, current and resistance. Today, all the functions are in one handy box with a rotary switch. Most devices show the value as a number on a display; older ones have a pointer.

The black lead goes into the **COM** socket, which stands for common. Depending on the measurement, the red lead goes into the socket for volts and ohms or for amperes. There is a separate 10A socket for large currents. On the rotary switch, V stands for voltage, A for current and the omega sign for resistance, with a straight line for direct current and a wavy line for alternating current.

**Voltage** is measured in parallel, so you hold the tips to two points, for example to the terminals of a battery. **Current** is measured in series: the current must flow through the device. Resistance is only measured without current, because the multimeter sends a small measuring current through itself. If you do not know the value, you start in the largest range and then switch down.

In a **continuity test**, the device beeps if there is a connection between two points. This lets you quickly find a broken cable or a blown fuse. A minus sign in front of the value shows that the leads are swapped, but with direct voltage this does no harm. Some devices also measure temperature or test diodes.

The units of the measured quantities are named after scientists. The volt recalls the Italian Alessandro Volta, who built the first battery. The ampere honours the Frenchman André-Marie Ampère, and the ohm the German Georg Simon **Ohm**. A fresh AA battery shows about 1.5 volts, a flat one clearly less.

A socket in Switzerland carries 230 volts of alternating voltage, which is life-threatening. Such measurements should only be made by experts with suitable devices. At school, you measure with batteries and small power supplies. Before every measurement, you check that the leads and tips are undamaged.

begriffe.erklaerung: The electrical pressure that drives the current, measured in volts.
How much electric charge flows per second, measured in amperes.
How strongly a component slows down the current, measured in ohms.
The range of values the device can measure at one setting.
A test to see whether a cable or wire is connected all the way through.

gewusst: For measuring voltage, a good multimeter has a very high internal resistance so that it hardly changes the circuit.
Devices set to measure current, on the other hand, have almost no resistance, which is why a wrong setting can destroy the built-in fuse.

teile.einleitung: An overhead line is a power cable stretched above railway tracks or streets that supplies trains, trams and trolleybuses with electricity. The vehicles pick up the current with a pantograph on the roof. In Switzerland, almost the entire railway runs on electricity from overhead lines.
wichtigste: Trains, trams and trolleybuses get their electricity from the overhead line.
The current is picked up by a pantograph on the roof of the locomotive.
On the railway, the current flows back through the rails.
The SBB's railway power has a frequency of 16.7 hertz.
Many Swiss trams run on around 600 volts direct voltage.
An overhead line is practically always live, even when no train is running.
Even getting close is life-threatening, because the current can jump across as an electric arc.
That is why you never climb onto parked goods wagons or fly kites near power lines.

abschnitte.text: The **overhead line**, also called the contact line on the railway, is a copper wire hanging above the tracks. It is held up by a carrier cable fixed to masts. The wire runs in a slight zigzag so that the pantograph wears evenly. Weights at the ends keep the wire taut in both heat and cold.

On the roof of the locomotive, a **pantograph** presses against the wire from below. The current flows through the motors and back through the wheels and **rails** to the substation. A trolleybus has no rails and so needs two wires and two poles. The SBB use alternating current at 15,000 volts and 16.7 hertz; trams mostly use around 600 volts direct current.

Switzerland has one of the densest **electrified** railway networks in the world. Because it had hardly any coal, it turned early on to electricity from hydropower. The SBB even run their own power stations and their own grid for railway power. Cities such as Zurich, Bern, Basel and Geneva also have tram and trolleybus lines with overhead lines.

An overhead line is practically always at **high voltage**, even when no train is running. At 15,000 volts you do not even have to touch the wire: the current can jump through the air as an **electric arc**. That is why climbing onto parked goods wagons or masts is life-threatening. A kite string or a long branch can also carry the current to a person.

A bird often sits on a single power line without coming to harm. There is almost no **voltage** between its two feet, so hardly any current flows through it. But if it touches something at a different voltage at the same time, such as an earthed mast, it is dangerous. For people, the rule is always: keep your distance.

begriffe.erklaerung: A frame on the roof of a vehicle that picks up current from the wire.
A hot, glowing flow of current through the air between two conductors.
How often alternating current changes direction per second, measured in hertz.
A facility that provides the current for the overhead line.
A bus with an electric motor that draws current from two overhead wires.

gewusst: At 16.7 hertz, the SBB's railway power has a different frequency from household power at 50 hertz, which is why the railway needs its own power grid.
When braking, modern locomotives can produce electricity and feed it back through the overhead line to other trains.

teile.einleitung: Optics is the branch of physics that deals with light. It explains how light travels, is reflected and refracted, and how lenses form images. Without optics there would be no glasses, cameras, microscopes or fibre-optic cables.
wichtigste: Optics is the study of light.
In a vacuum, light travels at exactly 299,792,458 metres per second.
When it passes into another material, light is refracted.
In a prism, violet light is refracted the most.
Converging lenses form images that can be calculated with the lens equation.
The power of a lens is measured in dioptres.
Short-sightedness is corrected with a diverging lens.

abschnitte.text: **Optics** studies light and how it behaves. **Geometric optics** represents light as straight rays and explains mirrors, lenses and shadows. Wave optics describes light as a wave and explains colours and interference. In a vacuum, light travels at exactly 299,792,458 metres per second.

When light passes at an angle from air into glass, it is refracted. Snell's **law of refraction** says n₁ · sin α = n₂ · sin β. If light hits glass with n = 1.5 at 30°, the angle of refraction is around 19.5°. Because different colours are refracted by different amounts, a **prism** splits white light, with violet being bent the most.

When light passes from glass into air, beyond a certain angle it cannot get out at all. It is then completely reflected back; this is called **total internal reflection**. For glass with n = 1.5, this **critical angle** is around 41.8°. Fibre-optic cables use total internal reflection to carry light and data over long distances.

A **converging lens** brings light together at the focal point. Where the image forms is calculated with the **lens equation** 1/f = 1/g + 1/b. If an object is 30 cm in front of a lens with a focal length of 10 cm, the image forms 15 cm behind the lens. The **power** of a lens is the reciprocal of its focal length in metres, so a lens with a focal length of 50 cm has 2 dioptres.

Our **eye** is an optical system with a cornea and a lens. In short-sightedness, the image forms in front of the retina, and a diverging lens corrects this. Cameras, binoculars, microscopes and telescopes are made of several lenses. In Switzerland, companies such as Leica in Heerbrugg have long been known for precision optical instruments.

begriffe.erklaerung: A number n that tells you how strongly a material bends light.
When light is completely reflected back at a boundary.
The distance between the lens and the focal point.
The unit of the power of a lens.

gewusst: The sparkle of diamonds comes from total internal reflection inside the stone.
Much of the internet runs through glass fibres, in which light signals travel.
Light takes only a little over a second to travel from the Moon to the Earth.

teile.einleitung: The mains frequency tells you how often the alternating current in the power grid changes direction back and forth each second. In Switzerland and almost all of Europe it is 50 hertz, in the USA 60 hertz. It has to be kept very precisely, otherwise there is a risk of a power cut.
wichtigste: In Switzerland and Europe, the mains frequency is 50 hertz.
In the USA, 60 hertz is usual; Japan has both frequencies.
In the European interconnected grid, all large generators turn in sync, so the frequency is the same everywhere.
If more electricity is used than produced, the frequency falls.
The spinning mass of the rotating generators softens rapid changes in frequency.
Primary control power reacts automatically within seconds.
If the frequency drops sharply, load is shed in stages to prevent a major blackout.

abschnitte.text: What comes out of the socket is **alternating current**, in which the direction of the current changes all the time. At 50 hertz, a full oscillation happens 50 times a second. The unit **hertz** is named after the German physicist Heinrich Hertz. The angular frequency of the 50 Hz grid is 2 · π · 50, around 314 per second.

Europe, Africa and large parts of Asia use 50 hertz, North and Central America mostly 60 hertz. Japan has a special situation: in the east of the country it is 50 hertz, in the west 60 hertz. This is because in the 19th century generators were bought there from Germany and from the USA. By the way, the Swiss railways use their own grid with 16.7 hertz.

The grid of continental Europe is a huge **interconnected grid** stretching from Portugal to Turkey. All the large generators in the power stations turn in exactly the same rhythm, that is **in sync**. That is why the mains frequency is the same everywhere, in Basel just as in Madrid. As early as 1958, the grids of Switzerland, Germany and France were connected at the “Star of Laufenburg” in Aargau.

The frequency shows whether exactly as much electricity is being produced as used. If suddenly more is used, the generators slow down a little and the frequency **falls**. If too much is produced, it rises. In the first moment after a power station fails, the **spinning mass** of the rotating generators softens the drop, like a heavy wheel that does not stop at once.

To keep the frequency at 50 hertz, power stations hold reserve power ready. **Primary control power** reacts automatically within seconds to any deviation. After that, secondary and tertiary control take over and balance out the deviation completely. In Switzerland, the national grid company Swissgrid coordinates these tasks.

If the frequency still drops sharply, a staged **load shedding** is triggered automatically. Individual areas or large users are briefly cut off from the grid. This prevents the whole grid from collapsing and causing a widespread blackout. Normally the frequency only varies by a few hundredths of a hertz.

begriffe.erklaerung: The unit of frequency, one oscillation per second.
Current that regularly changes direction.
At the same time and in the same rhythm.
Reserve power that power stations use to balance out fluctuations in the grid.
Deliberately switching off users in order to save the grid.

gewusst: Some alarm clocks and clocks count the oscillations of the grid and go wrong if the frequency is too low for a long time.
From the faint mains hum in sound recordings, experts can sometimes work out when a recording was made.
A generator with a single pair of poles has to turn 3000 times a minute to produce 50 hertz.

teile.einleitung: Optical density describes how strongly a transparent substance slows down and bends light. The optically denser a substance is, the more slowly light travels through it. That is why a stick in water looks bent and a swimming pool looks shallower than it really is.
wichtigste: Of two substances, the one with the higher refractive index is optically denser.
In the optically denser substance, light is slower than in the optically less dense one.
When light passes at an angle into an optically denser substance, it is bent towards the normal.
When light passes at an angle into an optically less dense substance, for example from glass into air, it is bent away from the normal.
Optical density and mass density are not the same: cooking oil floats on water but is optically denser.
Because of refraction, water looks shallower when seen from above.
Mirages over hot roads appear because hot air is optically less dense than cooler air.

abschnitte.text: Optical density tells you how strongly a substance slows down light. It is measured with the **refractive index** n. This tells you how much slower light is in the substance than in empty space, where it travels at about 300,000 kilometres per second. Air has a refractive index of almost exactly 1, water about 1.33, ordinary glass about 1.5 and diamond about 2.4.

When light hits the boundary between two substances at an angle, it changes direction. This is called **refraction**. As a helping line, you draw the **normal**, a line at right angles to the boundary surface. If the light enters the optically denser substance, it bends towards the normal; in the optically less dense substance, it bends away from it. If the light hits exactly at right angles, it carries straight on without bending.

If you hold a stick at an angle in water, it seems to bend at the surface. The light from the stick is refracted as it leaves the water, and our brain traces the light rays back in a straight line. That is why we see the stick in the wrong place. For the same reason, a pool 2 metres deep looks only about 1.5 metres deep from above, because the apparent depth is roughly the real depth divided by 1.33. So take care when swimming in a lake, because the water is deeper than it looks.

Many children think that a heavy substance is also optically dense, but that is not true. Cooking oil has a lower **mass density** than water and so floats on top. But its refractive index is about 1.47, which is greater than that of water. You can tell whether a substance is optically denser from the speed of light: if light is slower in substance A, at 200,000 kilometres per second, than in substance B, then A is optically denser.

Air can also have different optical densities, because warm air is optically slightly less dense than cold air. Over a hot road, light from the sky is therefore bent upwards, and it looks as if there were a puddle of water on the tarmac. This is called a **mirage**, or Fata Morgana. If light leaves an optically denser substance at a very shallow angle, it cannot get out at all and is completely reflected back. This **total internal reflection** is used in fibre-optic cables for the internet.

begriffe.erklaerung: A number that tells you how strongly a substance slows down and bends light.
An imaginary line at right angles to a boundary surface.
The change of direction of light when it passes from one substance into another.
Light is completely reflected at a boundary instead of passing out.
An apparent reflection caused by layers of air at different temperatures.

gewusst: Diamonds sparkle so much because their high refractive index makes light bounce back and forth inside them many times.
From under water, fish see the whole world above the lake through a circular window at the surface.
The Earth's atmosphere also bends light, which is why we can still see the Sun at sunset even though it is already just below the horizon.

teile.einleitung: A p-n junction is the boundary between two differently prepared regions of a semiconductor, for example made of silicon. It lets electric current through almost only in one direction. This makes it the heart of diodes, light-emitting diodes, solar cells and transistors in every mobile phone and computer.
wichtigste: A p-n junction forms where a p-doped and an n-doped semiconductor region meet.
At the boundary, a depletion region forms with hardly any free charge carriers.
The fixed ions at the boundary create the built-in voltage.
In the forward direction (positive terminal to p, negative terminal to n), the junction conducts.
In the reverse direction, the depletion region gets wider and only a tiny reverse current flows.
Above a threshold voltage, about 0.7 volts for silicon, the current in the forward direction rises sharply.
Diodes, LEDs, solar cells and varactor diodes are based on the p-n junction.

abschnitte.text: Pure **silicon** conducts electricity only poorly. Deliberately adding tiny amounts of foreign atoms to it is called **doping**. With phosphorus, you get an n-region with extra mobile electrons, that is negative charge carriers. With boron, you get a p-region with “holes”: missing electrons that behave like positive charges.

If you join a p-region and an n-region, electrons move across the boundary into the p-region because of the difference in concentration. This process is called **diffusion**. There they fill holes, and fixed, charged atoms are left behind on both sides. This creates a thin layer with almost no free charge carriers, the **depletion region**. The charges in it create the built-in voltage, which slows down any further movement.

If you connect the positive terminal to the p-region and the negative terminal to the n-region, the barrier layer is broken down and current flows. This is the **forward direction**. If you connect it the other way round, the depletion region gets wider and the junction blocks. Only a very small **reverse current** of minority carriers still flows. The characteristic curve shows that in the forward direction almost nothing flows until the threshold is reached, after which the current rises steeply.

The simplest use is the **diode**, a kind of one-way street for current, which rectifies alternating current in chargers, for example. In a light-emitting diode (LED), the electrons give off light as they cross. A solar cell does the opposite: light hits the junction and produces current. The varactor diode uses the fact that the width of the blocking zone, and so its capacitance, changes with the voltage, for example in radio receivers.

The American researcher Russell Ohl discovered the p-n junction in 1940 rather by chance on a silicon crystal. Shortly afterwards, William Shockley explained exactly what happens. Two p-n junctions one after the other led to the **transistor**, for which Shockley and colleagues received the Nobel Prize in 1956. Today a single computer chip contains billions of such junctions.

begriffe.erklaerung: A substance that sometimes conducts electricity well and sometimes badly, for example silicon.
Deliberately adding foreign atoms to change conductivity.
The boundary layer in a p-n junction where there are hardly any mobile charges.
A component that lets current through in one direction only.
A missing electron that moves like a positive charge.

gewusst: The colour of an LED depends on which semiconductor material its p-n junction is made of.
A solar panel on a Swiss roof is basically a huge, flat p-n junction.
The depletion region is often thinner than a thousandth of a millimetre.

teile.einleitung: Magnetic declination is the angle between the direction a compass needle points and the direction to the geographic North Pole. It exists because the magnetic North Pole is not in the same place as the geographic one. Another name for it is magnetic variation.
wichtigste: Magnetic declination is the angle between magnetic north and geographic north.
Another technical term for it is variation.
It changes over the years, because the Earth's magnetic poles move.
In Switzerland it is only a few degrees today.
Lines of equal declination on a map are called isogonic lines.
Sailors and pilots have to take it into account carefully when navigating.
Close to a magnetic pole, the declination can become very large.

abschnitte.text: A **compass needle** is a small magnet and lines itself up with the Earth's magnetic field. So it points to the magnetic North Pole, not exactly to the geographic North Pole around which the Earth turns. The angle between these two directions is called **magnetic declination** or variation. If the needle points east of geographic north, it is called easterly declination, otherwise westerly.

The Earth's magnetic field is created by currents of liquid iron deep inside the Earth. These currents change slowly, so the magnetic North Pole moves. For a long time it was in northern Canada, and for decades it has been moving towards Siberia. That is why the declination is different in every place and changes over time.

In Switzerland today, the compass needle points only a few degrees east of geographic north. For a hike with map and compass, this error is usually small. On accurate national maps, the declination is given at the edge of the map. About a hundred years ago, it was still westerly in Switzerland and clearly larger.

Lines connecting places with the same declination are called **isogonic lines**. The line on which the declination is zero is called the agonic line. Worldwide maps of declination are recalculated regularly because the magnetic field changes. Navigation devices and mobile phones use such models to work out true north from the compass direction.

Sailors and pilots must know the declination precisely, or they would drift far off course on long journeys. In addition, iron parts and electrical devices in the ship or aircraft deflect the needle. This deflection is called **deviation**. Both errors are added together when the course is calculated.

The closer you get to a magnetic pole, the larger the declination can become. In the Arctic, a compass needle can even point almost south or west. Right at the magnetic pole, the needle points steeply down into the ground. There, an ordinary compass is hardly usable for navigation.

begriffe.erklaerung: Another technical word for magnetic declination.
A line on a map connecting places with the same declination.
Deflection of the compass needle by iron or devices in the vehicle.
The place in the north that compass needles point to.

gewusst: At times the magnetic North Pole has moved several dozen kilometres a year.
Centuries ago, sailors already noticed that the compass does not point exactly north.
Runway numbers at airports are based on the magnetic direction and therefore sometimes have to be changed.

teile.einleitung: Instantaneous speed is the speed an object has at one particular moment. This is exactly the number that the speedometer in a car shows. It is often different from the average speed that you calculate for a whole journey.
wichtigste: Instantaneous speed is the speed at a particular moment.
A car's speedometer shows the instantaneous speed.
You measure it by dividing a very short distance by a very short time.
On a distance-time graph, it is the gradient of the curve at one point.
In uniform motion, it is always equal to the average speed.
A ball thrown upwards has an instantaneous speed of zero at its highest point.
A pendulum is fastest at its lowest point.

abschnitte.text: If a car travels 60 kilometres in 1 hour, its **average speed** is 60 km/h. But on the way it was sometimes faster, sometimes slower, and it stood still at traffic lights. The speed at a single moment is called the **instantaneous speed**. The speedometer shows it all the time.

You measure the distance an object travels in a very short time and divide it by that time. The shorter the time span, the more precisely you get the speed at that moment. An example: a car covers a 4-metre measuring section in 0.2 seconds, which is 20 m/s or 72 km/h. Some speed checks work this way too, with **light barriers** or sensors in the road.

On a distance-time graph, you record how far an object has travelled at each point in time. If the curve is steep, the object is fast; if it is flat, it is slow. You can see the instantaneous speed from the **gradient** of the curve at a particular point. In maths this is called the derivative, which Isaac Newton and Gottfried Wilhelm Leibniz developed in the 17th century.

Without air resistance, a falling stone becomes about 9.8 m/s faster every second. After 3 seconds, its instantaneous speed is 29.4 m/s, which is over 100 km/h. If you throw a ball straight up, it gets slower and slower. At its highest point, its instantaneous speed is exactly **zero** for a moment, and then it falls back down.

On a pendulum or a swing, the speed changes all the time. At the turning points right at the edges, it is briefly zero. At the lowest point, the instantaneous speed is greatest, because there most of the potential energy has been turned into kinetic energy. You can feel this on any swing as a brief tingle in your tummy.

On the road, it is always the instantaneous speed that counts, for example at a **speed camera**. Anyone caught doing 70 km/h in town cannot argue that they were only driving at 50 km/h on average. When skiing, cycling or in space travel, the speed at the moment is also important. Sports watches and mobile phones work it out, for example, with the help of GPS.

begriffe.erklaerung: Total distance divided by total time.
A display in a vehicle that shows the current speed.
Movement at an unchanging speed in the same direction.
How steeply a curve on a graph rises at one point.

gewusst: When a ball briefly stops at its highest point, gravity is still acting on it.
A speedometer usually shows a little more than you are actually doing, because it must never show too little.
A cheetah can run at over 90 km/h for a short moment, but can only keep up this speed for a few seconds.

teile.einleitung: The ohm is the unit of electrical resistance. It tells you how strongly a component or a wire slows down the electric current. Its symbol is the Greek letter omega, Ω, and it is named after the German physicist Georg Simon Ohm.
wichtigste: The ohm is the unit of electrical resistance.
Its symbol is the Greek letter omega, Ω.
It is named after the German physicist Georg Simon Ohm.
If exactly 1 ampere flows at 1 volt, the resistance is 1 Ω.
4.7 kilohms are 4700 Ω, 2 megohms are 2,000,000 Ω.
Resistance can be measured with a multimeter.
Coloured bands on small resistors show their value in ohms.

abschnitte.text: **Georg Simon Ohm** lived from 1789 to 1854 and came from Erlangen in Germany. For a long time he was a teacher of maths and physics and experimented with wires and electricity on the side. In 1826 and 1827 he published the law named after him, **Ohm's law**. At first his work was hardly noticed; later he became a professor in Munich.

When current flows through a wire, the electrons keep bumping into the atoms of the material and are slowed down. This braking effect is called **electrical resistance**. Copper has a low resistance and is good for cables. Rubber and plastic have an enormous resistance and are used as insulators.

Ohm's law links voltage, current and resistance: resistance equals voltage divided by current, in short R = U / I. A component through which exactly 1 ampere flows at 1 volt has a resistance of **1 ohm**. If only 1 ampere flows at 10 volts, it is 10 ohms. The greater the resistance, the smaller the current at the same voltage.

In electronics, large values are often needed, so there are multiples. A **kilohm** is 1000 Ω, so 4.7 kΩ is 4700 Ω. A megohm is a million ohms, so 2 MΩ is 2,000,000 Ω. Very small resistances, for example of thick cables, are given in milliohms.

Small components with a fixed resistance value are simply called **resistors**. They limit, for example, the current through a light-emitting diode so that it does not burn out. Their value is marked on them with coloured bands, the so-called colour code. Each colour stands for a digit, for example black for 0, brown for 1 and red for 2.

With a **multimeter** you can measure voltage, current and resistance. To measure resistance, you set the device to Ω and hold the two probe tips to the ends of the component. The device sends a small current through it and works out the resistance. This also lets you find out whether a cable is broken.

begriffe.erklaerung: How strongly a material or component slows down the current.
The rule that resistance equals voltage divided by current.
A measuring device for voltage, current and resistance.
A material that hardly conducts electricity at all.

gewusst: At very low temperatures, superconductors have no electrical resistance at all.
The human body also has an electrical resistance, which is much lower when the skin is wet than when it is dry.
The reciprocal of resistance is called conductance, and its unit used to be jokingly called the “mho”, ohm backwards.

teile.einleitung: Food energy is the energy contained in what we eat and drink. Our body needs it to grow, move and think, and even while sleeping to breathe and keep warm. Food packaging shows how much energy a product contains, usually in kilocalories and kilojoules.
wichtigste: The body needs energy for everything it does, even during sleep.
On packaging, energy is given in kilocalories and kilojoules.
Carbohydrates, fats and proteins provide energy.
Fat contains more than twice as much energy per gram as carbohydrates.
Nuts are particularly rich in energy.
Pure water contains no energy at all.
People who move a lot need more energy from their food.

abschnitte.text: Plants store the energy of sunlight in sugar and starch. When we eat plants or animals, our body takes in this stored energy. In the cells, it is released slowly with the help of oxygen, a bit like a very gentle burning. This is how muscles, brain and heart get the energy they need.

Energy is provided by three groups of nutrients. **Carbohydrates** are found in bread, pasta, rice and potatoes and give the body energy for everyday life. **Fats** in butter, oil and nuts provide about 9 kilocalories per gram, more than twice as much as carbohydrates or proteins with about 4 kilocalories. Water, vitamins and minerals are important but provide no energy.

On food packaging, the **nutrition table** shows how much energy there is in 100 grams. It is given in kilocalories, abbreviated kcal, and in kilojoules, abbreviated kJ. One kilocalorie is about 4.2 kilojoules. 100 grams of nuts often have over 600 kilocalories, 100 grams of apples only about 50.

abschnitte.titel: What the body needs energy for
abschnitte.text: Even when we sleep, the body needs energy for breathing, heartbeat and **body heat**; this is called the basal metabolic rate. On top of that comes energy for movement, sport and thinking, because the brain uses a lot of energy. Children also need extra energy to grow. A child playing football needs more energy than one sitting still.

Sweets give energy quickly but harm your teeth in large amounts and do not keep you full for long. Wholemeal bread, potatoes, vegetables and pulses release their energy more slowly and keep you full for longer. If you go a long time without eating, you feel tired and weak and find it hard to concentrate. The Swiss **food pyramid** shows how to eat a varied and balanced diet.

If you eat more energy than you use over a long time, the body stores it as fat. If you eat too little, you lack the strength to grow and learn. The best thing is a balance between eating and exercise. How much energy you need depends on your age, size and how much you move.

begriffe.erklaerung: A unit for the energy in food, abbreviated kcal.
The physical unit of energy, abbreviated kJ.
The energy the body needs when completely at rest.
Nutrients such as sugar and starch that provide energy quickly.
The table on the packet showing energy and nutrients.

gewusst: The brain makes up only about 2 per cent of body weight but uses around 20 per cent of the energy at rest.
You can measure the energy content of a food by burning it completely in a calorimeter and measuring the heat produced.
The body also uses extra energy when you are cold, because the shivering of the muscles produces heat.

teile.einleitung: Reverberation time tells you how long a sound keeps ringing in a room after the source of the sound has stopped. In an empty church, a clap echoes for a long time; in a room with carpet and curtains, hardly at all. The right reverberation time is very important for concert halls, classrooms and theatres.
wichtigste: Reverberation time is the time it takes for the sound level to fall by 60 decibels after the sound stops.
Wallace Clement Sabine founded scientific room acoustics around 1900.
According to Sabine's formula, T = 0.161 · V / A.
If you double the absorption area, the reverberation time is halved.
Large concert halls for symphonies have a reverberation time of about 2 seconds.
In classrooms, too long a reverberation time makes speech harder to understand.
Soft materials such as curtains, carpets and upholstery absorb sound.

abschnitte.text: Sound spreads out in a room and is **reflected** again and again by the walls, ceiling and floor. That is why you still hear a sound for a while even when the source is already silent. With each reflection, part of the sound is absorbed, until the sound disappears. The **reverberation time** measures how long it takes for the level to fall by 60 decibels, that is to a millionth of the sound intensity.

The American physicist **Wallace Clement Sabine** lived from 1868 to 1919 and taught at Harvard University. He was asked to improve a lecture hall in which the speakers could hardly be understood. Using seat cushions, a stopwatch and his own hearing, he studied how materials change the reverberation. From this, around 1900, he developed his formula and then advised on the building of Symphony Hall in Boston.

The formula is T = 0.161 · V / A, where V is the volume of the room in cubic metres and A is the **equivalent absorption area** in square metres. A room of 1000 m³ with 200 m² of absorption area has a reverberation time of about 0.8 seconds. The absorption area of a wall is its area times its absorption coefficient, so for 50 m² and 0.3 it is 15 m². If a room of 600 m³ is to have a reverberation time of 1.2 seconds, it needs about 80 m² of absorption area.

For symphonic music in large concert halls, people want about **2 seconds** of reverberation so that the music sounds full and warm. Large churches often echo much longer, which is lovely for organ music but difficult for speech. The concert hall in the KKL in Lucerne is famous worldwide for its very good acoustics. There, the acoustics can even be adapted to the music with movable flaps and chambers.

In classrooms, a short reverberation time of well under a second is important. If it is too long, the words blur together and **speech intelligibility** falls. Children then have to make more effort, and the room becomes louder overall. That is why acoustic ceilings, wall panels made of porous material or pinboards are fitted.

Hard, smooth surfaces such as concrete, glass and tiles reflect sound almost completely. Soft and porous materials such as carpets, curtains, upholstered furniture or acoustic foam **absorb** it. People absorb sound too, which is why a full hall sounds different from an empty one. You can try this at home by clapping your hands in an empty room and in a furnished room.

begriffe.erklaerung: The time in which a sound in a room becomes 60 decibels quieter.
The soaking up of sound by a material.
The unit for loudness, or sound level.
The study of how rooms sound.
The bouncing back of sound from a surface.

gewusst: A room with no reverberation, a so-called anechoic chamber, feels eerily silent to many people.
Because people absorb sound, concert seats are often upholstered so that the hall sounds similar whether it is empty or full.
The unit “sabin” for absorption area is named after Wallace Clement Sabine.

teile.einleitung: The ear is our sense organ for hearing and for balance. It turns tiny changes in air pressure, which we call sound, into electrical signals that the brain understands as notes, voices and music.
wichtigste: The ear consists of the outer ear, middle ear and inner ear.
The visible part of the ear is called the auricle or pinna.
The eardrum is a thin membrane that vibrates when sound arrives.
The middle ear contains the three ossicles: hammer, anvil and stirrup.
The stirrup is the smallest bone in the human body.
The cochlea in the inner ear looks like a snail shell and turns sound into nerve signals.
The inner ear also helps with balance.
With two ears, you can hear which direction a sound is coming from.

abschnitte.text: The outer ear includes the **auricle** and the **ear canal**. The auricle works like a small funnel that catches sound waves and directs them into the ear canal. In adults, the ear canal is about 2.5 centimetres long. At its end lies the eardrum, the boundary with the middle ear.

The **eardrum** is thinner than a sheet of paper and vibrates when sound hits it. It passes these vibrations on to the three **ossicles**: the hammer, anvil and stirrup. The ossicles act like a lever and amplify the movement. The stirrup is only about three millimetres long. The middle ear is connected to the throat by the **Eustachian tube**, which is why your ears pop when you swallow in an aeroplane or a cable car.

In the inner ear lies the **cochlea**, a coiled tube filled with fluid. The stirrup presses on a small window and sets the fluid moving. Fine **hair cells** sense this movement and send signals through the auditory nerve to the brain. High notes are detected at the start of the cochlea, low notes further in. A young person can hear sounds from about 20 to 20,000 vibrations per second.

Next to the cochlea lies the **organ of balance**. It consists of three semicircular canals filled with fluid that sense when the head turns. If you spin round quickly and then stop, the fluid keeps flowing for a moment. That is why you feel dizzy. Without this organ, we could hardly walk upright or ride a bike.

Because we have two ears, a sound from the side reaches one ear a tiny bit earlier and louder than the other. The brain analyses these tiny differences. This is how we can tell where a sound is coming from, for example a car that is approaching. This is called **directional hearing**. Many animals, such as owls, use this trick very precisely too.

**Earwax** protects the ear canal from dust, dirt and germs and moves outwards by itself. That is why you should not push cotton buds deep into your ear, because they push the wax inwards and can injure the eardrum. Very loud music, fireworks or machines can permanently damage the hair cells. These cells do not grow back. That is why **ear protection** and breaks from noise are important.

begriffe.erklaerung: A thin membrane at the end of the ear canal that is set vibrating by sound.
Hammer, anvil and stirrup, three tiny bones in the middle ear that pass on vibrations.
The coiled part of the inner ear in which sound is turned into nerve signals.
Three fluid-filled tubes in the inner ear that sense when the head turns.
A yellowish substance that cleans and protects the ear canal.

gewusst: The stirrup is about the size of a grain of rice.
Your ears keep hearing while you sleep, but the brain filters out most sounds.
Elephants hear very low notes that people cannot hear.

teile.einleitung: The Fukushima nuclear disaster was a serious accident at a Japanese nuclear power station in March 2011. A powerful earthquake and a huge tsunami knocked out the cooling of the reactors, and the fuel melted in three reactors. It was the worst nuclear accident since Chernobyl in 1986 and also had major consequences for energy policy in Switzerland.
wichtigste: The disaster began on 11 March 2011 at the Fukushima Daiichi nuclear power station in Japan.
It was triggered by a powerful earthquake followed by a tsunami.
The flood knocked out the power supply and the emergency diesel generators, so the cooling failed.
There was a meltdown in three reactor units.
Hydrogen explosions destroyed parts of the reactor buildings.
The power station was run by the company TEPCO.
Like Chernobyl, the accident was rated at the highest level, 7, on the international scale.

abschnitte.text: On 11 March 2011, a massive **earthquake** of magnitude 9 shook north-eastern Japan. Shortly afterwards, a **tsunami** rolled onto the coast: a huge flood wave that was over 13 metres high at the power station. The wave swept over the protective wall of the Fukushima Daiichi nuclear power station, which lies right on the Pacific. The earthquake and tsunami killed around 18,000 people in Japan altogether, most of them in the flood itself.

Even a reactor that has been shut down still produces a lot of heat for a long time and must be cooled constantly. Because of the earthquake, power from the grid failed first. Then the tsunami flooded the **emergency diesel generators** and the electrical equipment in the basement. Without electricity the pumps stopped working, and the cooling water gradually boiled away.

In reactor units 1, 2 and 3, the fuel rods became so hot that they melted; this is called a **meltdown**. This produced **hydrogen**, which got into the reactor buildings and exploded there. The explosions destroyed roofs and walls, and radioactive substances escaped into the air, soil and sea. The operator **TEPCO** and the authorities struggled for weeks to cool the reactors with water.

abschnitte.titel: Consequences for people and the environment
abschnitte.text: An exclusion zone was set up around the power station, and well over 100,000 people had to leave their homes. Some areas are still not habitable today; people have returned to others. The cooling water is treated, but radioactive **tritium** cannot be filtered out. Since 2023, the diluted, treated water has gradually been released into the Pacific, which is controversial in neighbouring countries. Dismantling the destroyed reactors will take decades more.

The disaster sparked debates worldwide about the safety of nuclear energy. In Switzerland, the Federal Council and Parliament decided in 2011 not to build any more new nuclear power stations. In 2017, voters approved the **Energy Strategy 2050**, which plans for more renewable energy and saving energy. The Mühleberg nuclear power station in the canton of Bern was shut down in 2019. In recent years, whether the ban on building new nuclear power stations should be relaxed again has become a political topic once more.

begriffe.erklaerung: A huge flood wave, usually caused by an earthquake under the sea.
An accident in which a reactor's fuel becomes so hot that it melts.
Invisible radiation given off by decaying atomic nuclei.
Diesel engines that supply electricity for important equipment during a power cut.
A radioactive form of hydrogen that cannot be filtered out of water.

gewusst: The name Daiichi means “number one” in Japanese; a few kilometres further south lies the Fukushima Daini plant, “number two”.
A reactor must be cooled for months even after it has been shut down, because the fuel keeps giving off heat.
Robots were later used in the exclusion zone to look inside the highly contaminated reactor buildings.

teile.einleitung: The Chernobyl nuclear disaster was one of the worst accidents ever at a nuclear power station. On 26 April 1986, unit 4 of the power station exploded in what was then the Soviet Union, in the area of today's Ukraine. Radioactive substances spread over large parts of Europe, as far as Switzerland.
wichtigste: The Chernobyl nuclear power station lies in the north of today's Ukraine.
The disaster happened during a safety test in unit 4.
The reactor that exploded was an RBMK reactor.
A positive void coefficient played a decisive part in the surge in power.
The accident was given the highest level, 7, on the international INES scale.
The nearby town of Pripyat was completely evacuated and is still abandoned today.
An exclusion zone with a radius of around 30 kilometres was set up around the power station.
In Switzerland, Ticino was the most heavily contaminated with radioactive caesium.

abschnitte.text: The **Chernobyl** nuclear power station lies close to the border with Belarus. In 1986 the area belonged to the Soviet Union; today it belongs to Ukraine. In the night of 25 to 26 April 1986, there was an explosion in **unit 4**. A few kilometres away lay the town of Pripyat, where many of the power station workers lived.

During the night, a **safety test** was carried out with several protective systems switched off. The **RBMK reactor** had a dangerous property: if steam bubbles formed in the cooling water, the power rose further. This positive void coefficient led to an extremely rapid surge in power. Steam and an explosion destroyed the reactor, and the graphite in the core burned for days.

Large amounts of **radioactive** substances escaped into the air. Firefighters and workers, later called liquidators, fought the fire and cleaned up. Several dozen of them died of radiation sickness in the first months. How many people later fell ill as a result is still disputed today.

The day after the accident, **Pripyat**, with around 50,000 inhabitants, was evacuated. People thought they would return after a few days, but the town is still abandoned today. An **exclusion zone** with a radius of around 30 kilometres was set up around the power station. A concrete shell, the sarcophagus, was first built over the destroyed reactor, and in 2016 a huge new protective shelter made of steel.

In the days that followed, winds carried the radioactive cloud across Europe. In Switzerland, there was heavy rain at the beginning of May 1986, especially in **Ticino**, so that is where the most **caesium-137** reached the ground. The authorities issued advice on foods such as vegetables and milk. Because caesium-137 has a half-life of around 30 years, it can still be detected today in soil, mushrooms and wild boar.

Chernobyl was the first accident to be given the highest level, 7, on the **INES** scale; Fukushima in Japan followed in 2011. The disaster led to better safety rules for nuclear power stations worldwide. In many countries, including Switzerland, there was intense debate about nuclear power afterwards. Today, many wild animals such as wolves, elk and wild horses live in the exclusion zone again.

begriffe.erklaerung: A power station that produces electricity by splitting atomic nuclei.
The property of some substances of giving off invisible, dangerous radiation.
The time after which half of a radioactive substance has decayed.
When people are quickly taken out of an area because of danger.
An area that you may not enter, or only with permission, because of danger.

gewusst: In Pripyat there is a Ferris wheel that was never properly used, because the funfair was only due to open after the accident.
The new shelter over the reactor is so big that a football stadium would fit underneath it, and it was slid over the reactor on rails.

teile.einleitung: Neutrinos are tiny elementary particles that have almost no mass and are electrically neutral. Every second, billions of them fly through your body without you noticing anything. Because they so rarely collide with other matter, they are sometimes called “ghost particles”.
wichtigste: Neutrinos are electrically neutral elementary particles with a tiny mass.
They interact only very weakly and so pass almost unhindered through the whole Earth.
Around 60 billion neutrinos from the Sun hit every square centimetre of the Earth each second.
They were first detected directly in 1956 at a nuclear reactor.
Neutrino oscillations prove that neutrinos have mass.
Large detectors such as IceCube at the South Pole or Super-Kamiokande in Japan track them down.
In 1987, neutrinos from an exploding star were measured for the first time, from supernova 1987A.

abschnitte.text: In 1930, physicists had a puzzle: in radioactive beta decay, energy seemed to disappear. The Austrian physicist **Wolfgang Pauli**, then a professor at ETH Zurich, therefore suggested an unknown, neutral particle that carries away the missing energy. The Italian Enrico Fermi gave it the name neutrino, which means “little neutral one”. Pauli himself feared that this particle would never be detected.

Neutrinos are **elementary particles**, which means they are not made of even smaller parts. They have no electric charge and a mass much smaller than that of an electron. They only feel the weak nuclear force and gravity. That is why they fly through walls, mountains and even the whole Earth as if nothing were there.

It was not until 1956 that the Americans Clyde Cowan and Frederick Reines managed to detect neutrinos directly. They placed their detector next to a **nuclear reactor**, which produces huge numbers of neutrinos. Only very rarely did one of them collide with a particle in the detector. Reines received the Nobel Prize in Physics for this in 1995.

There are three kinds of neutrino: electron, muon and tau neutrinos. On their way, they can change from one kind into another; this is called **neutrino oscillation**. This is only possible if neutrinos have mass. Takaaki Kajita and Arthur McDonald received the Nobel Prize in Physics for this discovery in 2015.

Because neutrinos react so rarely, you need huge detectors. **Super-Kamiokande** in Japan lies deep in a mine and is filled with ultra-pure water, in which neutrinos sometimes cause faint flashes of light, Cherenkov light. **IceCube** at the South Pole uses a whole cubic kilometre of ice with thousands of light sensors. Such facilities lie deep underground or in the ice so that other particles do not interfere.

Neutrinos are produced in large numbers in the Sun, where hydrogen fuses into helium. In 1987, neutrinos from an exploding star were measured for the first time, from **supernova 1987A** in a neighbouring galaxy of the Milky Way. In 2011, neutrinos sent from CERN near Geneva to Gran Sasso in Italy seemed to be faster than light. But the cause was a measuring error, including a badly fitted fibre-optic connector.

begriffe.erklaerung: A particle that is not made of smaller parts.
A kind of radioactive decay in which neutrinos are also produced.
The change of a neutrino into another kind of neutrino.
A measuring device that tracks down particles.
The enormous explosion of a large star.

gewusst: The human body also sends out neutrinos, because it contains tiny amounts of radioactive substances such as potassium.
Neutrinos from the Sun reach us at night too; they simply fly right through the whole Earth.
Wolfgang Pauli presented his neutrino idea in 1930 in a letter addressed to “Dear radioactive ladies and gentlemen”.

teile.einleitung: Surface tension is a property of liquids that makes their surface behave like a thin, stretched skin. That is why drops of water are round and small insects can walk across a pond. You can easily watch it for yourself with a coin and a pipette.
wichtigste: Surface tension holds the surface of a liquid together like a skin.
It arises because particles at the surface are only pulled inwards.
It is given in the unit newtons per metre.
At 20 degrees, water has a surface tension of around 73 millinewtons per metre.
Washing-up liquid lowers the surface tension of water.
As the temperature rises, the surface tension decreases.
Mercury has a much higher surface tension than water.

abschnitte.text: Every liquid is made of tiny particles, the **molecules**, which attract each other. Inside the liquid, a molecule is pulled equally strongly from all sides. But at the surface there are no neighbours above, so these molecules are only pulled **inwards**. This makes the liquid try to keep its surface as small as possible, and a kind of stretched skin forms.

For a simple experiment, you clean and dry a coin and lay it down flat. Then, with a pipette, you slowly and carefully drip water onto it so that the water skin does not break. A surprisingly high, curved **hill of water** forms. Only when there are too many drops does the water overflow, and you write down how many drops fitted.

For the same volume, a **sphere** has the smallest surface. That is why small drops of water form perfect spheres in weightlessness, for example on the space station. Soap bubbles are round too, and inside them there is a slight excess pressure. For a soap bubble with a radius of 2 centimetres, it is only about 5 pascals.

Washing-up liquid and soap contain **surfactants**, which gather at the surface of the water and greatly lower the surface tension. That is why water with washing-up liquid can get into fibres and cracks better and loosen dirt. Heat also lowers the surface tension, which is why hot water cleans better. Mercury, on the other hand, has a much higher surface tension than water and forms shiny little balls.

The **pond skater** is an insect that can glide over ponds without sinking, thanks to surface tension. A metal paper clip laid down carefully can also stay lying on water. Plants use surface tension, together with other forces, to carry water upwards in fine tubes. Morning dew forms small round drops on leaves.

begriffe.erklaerung: A tiny particle that a substance is made of.
A substance in soap that lowers surface tension.
An insect that can walk on the surface of water.
The unit in which surface tension is measured.

gewusst: If you put a drop of washing-up liquid next to a floating paper clip, it suddenly sinks, because the water skin gives way.
Without surface tension, you could not make soap bubbles.
Water has one of the highest surface tensions of all ordinary liquids.

teile.einleitung: A marble run is a track on which small balls, the marbles, roll down through channels, bends and tunnels. You can buy one or simply build one yourself out of cardboard. While doing so, you learn a lot in a playful way about gravity, speed and friction.
wichtigste: On a marble run, marbles roll along: small balls made of glass, wood or clay.
For a marble to roll by itself, the track must slope downwards.
You can easily build your own marble run from cardboard tubes.
On bends, the track needs high edges, or fast marbles fly out.
If a marble has to roll uphill, it slows down.
On a flat carpet, the marble slows down and comes to a stop.
Lots of zigzag bends make the ride long.

abschnitte.text: A **marble run**, also called a ball track, is made of channels, tubes or building blocks with grooves. You put a **marble** in at the top, and it comes out again at the bottom. On the way, it rolls through bends, tunnels, funnels and sometimes over switches. In Switzerland, marbles are also called Chlicker.

**Gravity** always pulls the marble downwards. If the track slopes, the ball rolls downhill and gets faster. The steeper the slope, the faster it gets. If it has to go uphill for a bit, it slows down and only makes it if it has enough momentum.

A fast marble wants to keep going straight on at a bend. High edges or banked bends keep it on the track, like on a bobsleigh run. On a flat carpet, **friction** slows the ball down until it stops. On smooth wood or plastic, it rolls much further.

You can build your own track out of **cardboard tubes** from kitchen roll, sticky tape and a wall. You cut the tubes open lengthways and stick them below each other at a slant and in a zigzag. The more bends, the longer the marble is on its way. With a stopwatch, you can measure which design gives the longest ride.

The Swiss company **Cuboro** makes well-known marble runs out of wooden cubes. Grooves and tunnels are milled into the cubes, which can be put together in new ways again and again. There are also plastic systems and huge marble runs in museums and playgrounds. While building, you practise planning, trying things out and working carefully.

Around 400 years ago, the scientist **Galileo Galilei** rolled balls down sloping channels. In this way he studied how objects get faster and faster as they fall. On a marble run, you can see how height is turned into movement. If, for example, 3 red and 4 blue marbles roll, that makes 7 altogether, and you can hold races between them.

begriffe.erklaerung: A small ball made of glass, clay, wood or stone for playing with.
The force with which the Earth pulls everything downwards.
A force that slows down movement when two things rub against each other.
How steeply a track is tilted downwards.

gewusst: Marbles are among the oldest toys in the world; children in ancient Egypt and ancient Rome already played with them.
On a track, a marble never quite rolls back up to the same height it started from, because friction always takes away some energy.

teile.einleitung: A mobile is a hanging, moving work of art made of rods, threads and figures that float in balance. Even a light draught makes it turn and sway. The American artist Alexander Calder made this art form famous.
wichtigste: A mobile is a hanging, moving work of art.
The name comes from “mobile”, which means able to move.
Alexander Calder made the mobile famous in the 1930s.
A draught sets a mobile moving without a motor.
For a mobile to hang level, the weights must balance according to the law of the lever.
If a rod hangs at a slant, you move the hanging thread closer to the heavier figure.
A mobile often hangs above a baby's cot.

abschnitte.text: A mobile is made of several horizontal rods with figures or more rods hanging from their ends. Everything hangs on threads from the ceiling. The parts turn freely and do not touch each other. Because the picture keeps changing, the mobile is also called **kinetic art**, which means art of movement.

The American artist **Alexander Calder** lived from 1898 to 1976. He had first studied mechanical engineering and so understood balance and technology. In the early 1930s, he built his first hanging works of art from wire and painted sheet metal in Paris. The artist Marcel Duchamp gave them the name “mobile”.

Each rod of a mobile is a **lever** that hangs from its thread as if from a pivot. It hangs level when weight times distance is the same on both sides. So two fish of equal weight at the same distance from the middle keep the rod level. If one figure is heavier, it has to hang closer to the hanging point, which is why you move the thread towards the heavy side.

A mobile does not need a motor. A light **draught** from an open window or warm rising air is enough. Because the parts are so finely balanced, a tiny force is enough to make them turn. The movements are slow and calm, which is why mobiles often have a soothing effect.

Many parents hang a mobile above a baby's cot. Babies enjoy following the shapes and colours with their eyes. Mobiles also hang as decorations in classrooms, shops and museums. Large mobiles by Calder hang, for example, in museums and entrance halls in the USA and in Europe.

You can make a simple mobile from **twigs**, threads and paper figures. It is best to start at the bottom with the smallest rod and balance it. Then you hang this part from a larger rod and balance it again. This way, a floating work of art grows level by level.

begriffe.erklaerung: A rod that moves around a pivot and can balance forces.
A state in which all forces cancel each other out and nothing tips over.
Works of art that move.
The point a lever turns around; in a mobile, the hanging thread.

gewusst: As a young man, Calder also built a small circus out of wire, with which he gave performances.
Calder's counterparts to mobiles, which stand firmly on the ground, are called stabiles.
Some of Calder's mobiles are several metres in size and weigh hundreds of kilograms.

teile.einleitung: Muscle power is the force that people and animals produce with their muscles. We use it to walk, jump, lift and breathe. Long before there were engines, the muscle power of people and animals was the most important driving force in the world.
wichtigste: We move our bodies with our muscles.
Humans have more than 600 muscles.
Most muscles are attached to the bones by tendons.
Muscles can only pull, not push, which is why they work in pairs.
The heart is a muscle that works without a break for a whole lifetime.
The largest human muscle is the gluteus maximus, the big buttock muscle.
A bicycle without a motor is driven by muscle power alone.

abschnitte.text: A muscle is made up of many long **muscle fibres** that can contract. As they do, the muscle becomes shorter and thicker and pulls on a bone. The commands for this come from the brain through the nerves. The muscle gets the energy for this from food and from the oxygen that the blood brings.

Most muscles are attached to the bones by **tendons**. Because muscles can only pull, there is always an opposing muscle. The **biceps** on the upper arm bends the arm, and the triceps on the back straightens it again. Bones and joints act like levers, very much as in physics.

We move skeletal muscles on purpose, for example when walking or throwing. Smooth muscles work by themselves, for example in the stomach and intestines. A special kind is the **heart muscle**, which pumps around the clock without getting tired. In children at rest, it beats about 80 to 100 times a minute.

Humans have more than 600 muscles; in adults they make up about a third to almost half of body weight. The largest is the **gluteus maximus**, the big buttock muscle, which helps us stand up and climb stairs. The smallest muscle is in the ear and is only a few millimetres long. For their size, the chewing muscles are among the strongest muscles.

A bicycle, a rowing boat or a scooter without a motor runs on muscle power alone. In the past, horses and oxen pulled ploughs and carts, and people carried heavy loads on their backs. In Switzerland, muleteers carried goods with mules over Alpine passes such as the Gotthard. Muscle power is clean and quiet and produces no exhaust fumes.

If you do sport regularly, you make your muscles stronger and give them more stamina. After an unusual amount of exercise, you often feel **sore muscles** the next day. This is caused by tiny injuries in the muscle fibres, which the body repairs within a few days. Enough sleep, protein in your food and warming up before sport help the muscles.

begriffe.erklaerung: A long, thin cell that can contract.
A tough band that connects a muscle to a bone.
A muscle that reverses the movement of another muscle.
Pain in the muscles after unusual effort.

gewusst: Breathing also happens with muscle power, because the diaphragm contracts and lets air flow into the lungs.
Dozens of muscles are also at work at the same time when you speak.
The tongue is made almost entirely of muscles.

teile.einleitung: The mixing temperature is the temperature reached when you bring a warm and a cold substance together. If you mix hot and cold water, the result lies somewhere in between. With a simple rule, you can work out exactly where.
wichtigste: The basis is that the heat given off equals the heat taken in.
Equal masses of water at 20 and 60 degrees together give 40 degrees.
The rule for calculating it is named after the physicist Georg Wilhelm Richmann.
The mixing temperature depends on mass, temperature and specific heat capacity.
Water has a very large heat capacity and therefore strongly affects the mixture.
If ice melts in the mixture, extra heat of fusion is needed.
Calculations usually ignore heat lost to the surroundings.

abschnitte.text: When two objects at different temperatures come together, **heat** flows from the warm one to the cold one. This continues until both are equally warm. This shared final temperature is called the **mixing temperature**. It always lies between the two starting temperatures.

The physicist **Georg Wilhelm Richmann** lived in Saint Petersburg in the 18th century. He realised that the heat given off by the warm substance is exactly as large as the heat taken in by the cold one. This leads to **Richmann's mixing rule**. For each substance you multiply mass, heat capacity and temperature, and divide the sum by the sum of mass times heat capacity.

With equal amounts of water, the mixture is exactly in the middle: 20 and 60 degrees give 40 degrees. If you mix 2 kilograms at 10 degrees with 1 kilogram at 70 degrees, you get 30 degrees. 30 litres at 50 degrees and 10 litres at 10 degrees give 40 degrees. The more there is of one kind, the closer the mixture is to its temperature.

Not every substance stores the same amount of heat. This is described by the **specific heat capacity**: for water around 4180 joules per kilogram and degree, for iron only around 450.
