If you drop 0.1 kilograms of iron at 200 degrees into 0.3 kilograms of water at 20 degrees, the water only rises to about 26 degrees. Even with 1 kilogram of hot water and 1 kilogram of cold copper, the mixture is close to the water temperature.

If you put ice into warm water, the ice first has to melt. This needs the **heat of fusion**, 334 kilojoules per kilogram for ice, without the temperature rising. That is why ice cubes cool a drink so well. 0.1 kilograms of ice in 0.5 kilograms of water at 40 degrees end up at only about 20 degrees.

If you want a bath at 37 degrees and have 50 litres of water at 15 degrees, you need around 48 litres of water at 60 degrees. The rule also helps with tea and cold milk or when cooling a baby's bottle. In reality, some heat is always lost to the air and the container. In the laboratory, it is therefore measured in a well-insulated container, the **calorimeter**.

begriffe.erklaerung: Energy that flows from a warmer object to a colder one.
How much energy is needed to warm 1 kilogram of a substance by 1 degree.
Energy needed to melt a solid substance.
A well-insulated container in which amounts of heat are measured.

gewusst: Because water can store so much heat, large lakes such as Lake Geneva bring milder winters to their shores.
Georg Wilhelm Richmann was killed in 1753 during an experiment with lightning.

teile.einleitung: Newton's law of gravitation describes how strongly two masses attract each other. It explains why an apple falls from a tree and why the Moon circles the Earth. Isaac Newton published it in 1687, linking heaven and Earth in a single rule.
wichtigste: The larger the masses, the more strongly they attract each other.
If you double both masses, the force becomes four times as large.
If you triple the distance, the force falls to a ninth.
The apple pulls on the Earth exactly as strongly as the Earth pulls on the apple.
Spherically symmetrical celestial bodies can be treated like point masses at their centre.
The force between the Earth and the Moon is about 2 times 10 to the power of 20 newtons.
The law could not fully explain the precession of Mercury's perihelion.

abschnitte.text: Two objects attract each other with a force that is proportional to both **masses**. At the same time, the force decreases with the square of the distance. The formula is F equals G times m1 times m2 divided by r squared. G is the **gravitational constant**, a very small number of about 6.67 times 10 to the power of minus 11.

If you double both masses, the force becomes two times two, so four times as large. If you triple one mass and halve the distance, the force rises to twelve times as much. The distance is always measured between the centres. This holds exactly for planets if they are **spherically symmetrical**.

**Isaac Newton** wondered whether the same force moves the apple and the Moon. The Moon is around 60 Earth radii from the centre of the Earth. According to the law, its acceleration should therefore be only 1/3600 of the acceleration due to gravity on Earth. That matched its orbit exactly, and Newton published the law in 1687 in his work **Principia**.

According to Newton's third law, the apple pulls on the Earth just as strongly as the other way round. But because the Earth is enormous, you do not notice it move. Since the force is proportional to mass, all objects fall equally fast without air. In 1971, the astronaut David Scott dropped a hammer and a feather on the Moon, and both landed at the same time.

In 1798, the Englishman Henry **Cavendish** used a delicate torsion balance to measure the attraction between lead balls. This made it possible to determine G and even to calculate the mass of the Earth. Using the law, astronomers predicted the planet Neptune in 1846 before anyone had seen it. Only the small **precession of the perihelion** of Mercury remained a mystery; it was not explained until Einstein's general theory of relativity of 1915.

The pull of the Moon and the Sun on the oceans causes the **tides**. Satellites and the International Space Station stay in their orbits thanks to gravity. The paths of space probes are also calculated with Newton's law. The attraction between two people, on the other hand, is so tiny that you cannot feel it.

begriffe.erklaerung: The force of attraction between all objects that have mass.
A fixed number G that tells you how strong gravity is.
How much matter an object has, measured in kilograms.
The slow shifting of the point of a planet's orbit closest to the Sun.

gewusst: Newton is said to have got the idea from a falling apple in his family's garden, but whether the story is exactly true is uncertain.
If the Earth were only half as big but had the same mass, you would be four times as heavy on its surface.

teile.einleitung: Moonlight is the light that reaches us from the Moon at night. But the Moon does not shine by itself; it only reflects sunlight like a big grey mirror. At full moon it is so bright that you can even cast a faint shadow outdoors.
wichtigste: The Moon does not shine by itself; it reflects sunlight.
Moonlight is brightest at full moon.
At new moon, you cannot see the Moon in the sky at all.
Moonlight is much weaker than sunlight.
Light from the Moon takes about one second to reach the Earth.
You cannot get sunburnt in moonlight, because it is too weak.
From the Earth we always see the same side of the Moon.

abschnitte.text: The Moon is a lump of rock with no light of its own. What we see as **moonlight** is sunlight reflected from its surface. The rock is rather dark grey and reflects only a small part of the light, roughly as much as old asphalt. Even so, the Moon looks brilliantly bright against the dark night sky. The light takes only about **one second** to cover the roughly 384,000 kilometres to the Earth.

Moonlight is brightest at **full moon**, when the whole side facing us is lit. At **new moon** we see the unlit side and the Moon is practically invisible. But even the full moon is several hundred thousand times fainter than the Sun. On a clear full-moon night, the light is still enough to cast a faint shadow and to make out your surroundings on a path.

In weak moonlight, our eyes mainly use the **rods**, which tell light from dark but hardly see colours. That is why a moonlit landscape looks almost black and white or slightly bluish. You cannot get sunburnt in moonlight, because it contains far too little ultraviolet radiation. If you go walking at night, it is best to let your eyes get used to the dark without a torch.

The Moon turns once on its own axis in exactly the same time that it takes to orbit the Earth. That is why it always shows us the same side, which is called **tidal locking**. People first saw the far side of the Moon in 1959, in photos from a Soviet space probe. On the near side you can see dark patches with the naked eye, the so-called **maria**, which were once thought to be seas.

Many animals are guided by moonlight, for example nocturnal birds and insects that use it to find their way. In the past, the full moon was important for people because they could travel or work on bright nights. On some clear nights, a **moonbow** even appears, which looks almost white to our eyes. Because of all the artificial lighting in towns, people notice moonlight less today than in the countryside or in the mountains.

begriffe.erklaerung: The phase of the Moon in which the whole visible side of the Moon is lit.
The phase of the Moon in which you cannot see the Moon.
The Moon turns in such a way that it always shows the Earth the same side.
Dark, flat plains on the Moon made of solidified lava.

gewusst: The Moon is actually quite dark; its rock reflects only about an eighth of the sunlight.
When we look at the Moon, we see it as it was just over a second ago.
When there is a thin crescent moon, you can sometimes see the dark part glowing faintly, because light from the Earth falls on it.

teile.einleitung: Newton's theory of colour is the explanation by the English scientist Isaac Newton that white light is made up of many colours. Around 1666, he used glass prisms to split sunlight into a band of rainbow colours. His experiments are seen as the beginning of modern colour research.
wichtigste: Newton showed that white light is made up of many colours.
Around 1666, he split sunlight into a spectrum with a prism.
A single spectral colour could not be split any further by a second prism.
With a prism placed the other way round, he combined the colours back into white light.
Newton divided the spectrum into seven colours, adding indigo to do so.
In 1704, he published his findings in the book “Opticks”.
In 1810, Johann Wolfgang von Goethe criticised Newton in his work “Theory of Colours”.

abschnitte.text: Around 1666, the University of Cambridge had to close because of the plague, and the young **Isaac Newton** carried on his research at home. He let a narrow beam of sunlight fall through a small hole in the window shutter onto a triangular piece of glass, a **prism**. On the wall, there was no white spot but a long coloured band from red to violet. This band of colours is called a **spectrum**.

Newton wanted to know whether the prism makes the colours or whether they are already in the light. He sent a single colour through a second prism, and it stayed the same and was not split any further. Then he placed a second prism the other way round and combined all the colours back into white light. This proved that white light is a mixture of all the spectral colours.

abschnitte.titel: Seven colours and the colour wheel
abschnitte.text: Newton divided the spectrum into seven colours: red, orange, yellow, green, blue, **indigo** and violet. He chose the number seven because he compared the colours with the seven notes of the musical scale. To show how colours mix, he arranged them in a **colour wheel**. Colour wheels like this are still used in art and design today.

Newton published his findings about light and colours in 1704 in the book **“Opticks”**. In it, he described light as a stream of tiny particles. He also explained why lenses in telescopes produce coloured edges. That was why, as early as 1668, he had built a reflecting telescope that avoids this problem.

The poet **Johann Wolfgang von Goethe** did not agree with Newton. In 1810 he published his own work, “Theory of Colours”, and argued that colours arise from the interplay of light and darkness. In physics, Newton's explanation won. But Goethe's observations about how people perceive and feel colours are still interesting for art and psychology today.

Newton's theory of colour explains how a **rainbow** forms: water drops act like little prisms and split the sunlight. Splitting light led to spectroscopy, which is used today to find out what stars are made of. Screens and cameras also rely on mixing colours of light. So Newton's experiments with simple glass prisms still have an effect in modern technology.

begriffe.erklaerung: A triangular piece of glass that bends light and splits it into colours.
The band of colours produced when light is split.
A pure colour of the spectrum that cannot be split any further.
A circular arrangement of colours that shows how they are related.

gewusst: Newton included indigo mainly so that he would end up with exactly seven colours.
Newton was only in his early twenties when he did his famous prism experiments.
A rainbow always shows the colours in the same order, with red on the outside and violet on the inside.

teile.einleitung: Fog is a cloud that lies right on the ground. It is made of countless tiny droplets of water that float in the air and make it hard to see. In the Swiss Plateau, fog is so common in autumn and winter that people often talk about a “sea of fog”.
wichtigste: Fog is made of tiny water droplets floating in the air.
It is called fog when visibility falls below one kilometre.
Very light fog with better visibility is called mist.
Fog often forms in the morning over lakes and rivers.
When the Sun warms it up, fog often clears.
In fog, drivers should drive more slowly and leave a bigger gap.
Ships warn each other in thick fog with a foghorn.

abschnitte.text: Air always contains invisible **water vapour**. When the air cools down, it can hold less water vapour, and this condenses into tiny droplets. If these droplets float close to the ground, fog forms. Meteorologists call it fog when visibility falls below one kilometre, otherwise **mist**.

On clear, still nights, the ground cools down a lot, and so does the air above it. This creates **radiation fog**, especially in valleys and hollows. The air over lakes and rivers is damp, which is why fog often forms there in the morning. Fog also forms when warm, damp air flows over cold ground or cold water, for example on sea coasts.

abschnitte.titel: Sea of fog over the Swiss Plateau
abschnitte.text: In autumn and winter, a blanket of fog often lies over the Swiss Plateau for days. Cold air collects between the Jura and the Alps, with warmer air lying above it like a lid; this is called an **inversion**. If the fog does not lie on the ground but a few hundred metres higher up, it is called **high fog**. Anyone who climbs the Uetliberg, Pilatus or the Napf then often sees a beautiful sea of fog in the sunshine.

Fog is dangerous because you only see obstacles and other vehicles late. Drivers should therefore drive more slowly, switch on their lights and increase the **gap** to the car in front. Cars have special fog lights that may only be used in thick fog. At airports, taking off and landing in very thick fog is sometimes difficult, but modern instruments help the pilots.

Ships warn each other in thick fog with a loud **foghorn**. In the past, there were foghorns and bells at lighthouses on dangerous coasts. Today, radar and satellite navigation also help to avoid collisions. On Swiss lakes, passenger boats travel slowly in fog and give sound signals.

On foggy mornings, spider webs suddenly become easy to see, because many tiny water drops cling to the threads. When the Sun warms up the fog, the droplets evaporate and it clears. In fog, sounds seem muffled and the landscape looks mysterious. In some dry parts of the world, people even collect drinking water from fog with nets.

begriffe.erklaerung: When water vapour cools down and turns into liquid droplets.
Light fog in which you can still see more than a kilometre.
Fog that lies like a grey blanket above the ground.
A weather situation in which cold air lies below and warmer air above it.

gewusst: Fog and clouds are made of exactly the same thing; fog is just on the ground.
In the Atacama Desert in Chile and on other dry coasts, nets catch fog droplets as water.
When you walk in fog, your clothes can get wet even though it is not raining at all.

teile.einleitung: The Moon is the Earth's only natural companion and our nearest neighbour in space. It is much smaller than the Earth, and its gravity is only about one sixth as strong. In 1969, with Apollo 11, people walked on its surface for the first time.
wichtigste: On average, the Moon is about 384,000 kilometres from the Earth.
It is about a quarter as wide as the Earth.
Its gravity is only about one sixth of the gravity on Earth.
It takes about four weeks to go once around the Earth.
It has almost no air, because its gravity is too weak.
The Moon's pull causes the tides on Earth.
In 1969, with Apollo 11, the first people landed on the Moon.

abschnitte.text: The Moon has a diameter of about 3474 kilometres, making it about **a quarter as wide** as the Earth. On average it is around **384,000 kilometres** away. Light takes only just over a second to travel this distance. The Moon orbits the Earth in about four weeks and always shows us the same side.

Because the Moon is much smaller and lighter than the Earth, its **gravity** is only about one sixth as strong. A bathroom scale that shows 30 kg on Earth would show only about 5 kg on the Moon. A stone falls more slowly there, and astronauts could make long jumps. The weak gravity can hardly hold on to any air either, which is why the Moon has almost no **atmosphere**.

The large dark areas are called **lunar seas**, even though there is no water there. They are made of solidified lava from the Moon's early days. The bright areas are highlands full of **craters**, which were formed by rocks crashing into them. During the day it gets hotter than 100 °C on the Moon, and at night far colder than 100 °C below zero. Because there is neither wind nor rain, footprints stay for a very long time.

The Moon's pull tugs at the Earth's oceans and creates the **tides**. Depending on how the Sun lights up the Moon, we see it as a full moon, half moon or new moon. These **phases of the Moon** repeat about every 29.5 days. Scientists think that the Moon formed about 4.5 billion years ago after a huge collision between another body and the young Earth.

On 20 July 1969, the **Apollo 11** mission landed in the Sea of Tranquillity. **Neil Armstrong** was the first person to step onto the Moon, followed shortly afterwards by Buzz Aldrin. By 1972, a total of twelve astronauts had been on the Moon. Together they brought several hundred kilograms of moon rock back to Earth.

As the first scientific experiment, Buzz Aldrin set up a **solar wind sail** from the University of Bern. It was a kind of aluminium foil that caught particles from the solar wind. The experiment was led by the Bern physicist **Johannes Geiss**. The Bern sail was also taken along on later Apollo flights.

begriffe.erklaerung: The changing shapes in which we see the lit part of the Moon.
A round hollow formed by an impact.
A large dark plain of solidified lava on the Moon.
The regular rising and falling of the sea level.

gewusst: The Moon moves about 3.8 centimetres further away from the Earth every year.
The far side of the Moon was not photographed until 1959, by a Soviet space probe.
On the Moon, the sky is black even during the day, because there is no air to scatter the light.

teile.einleitung: Otto von Guericke was a German natural scientist, inventor and mayor of Magdeburg in the 17th century. He invented the air pump and proved with spectacular experiments that empty space, the vacuum, really exists. His Magdeburg hemispheres, which not even horses could pull apart, are famous.
wichtigste: Otto von Guericke lived from 1602 to 1686.
He was mayor of his home town of Magdeburg.
Around 1650 he invented the air pump.
With the Magdeburg hemispheres, he showed the enormous force of air pressure.
He disproved the old teaching that there can be no empty space.
With a ball of sulphur, he built an early machine that produced electricity.
The University of Magdeburg is named after him today.

abschnitte.text: Otto Gericke was born in Magdeburg in 1602 and studied law and mathematics, among other subjects. In the **Thirty Years' War**, Magdeburg was captured in 1631 and almost completely destroyed. Guericke survived and then helped rebuild the town as an engineer. From 1646 he was **mayor** of Magdeburg for many years, and later he was made a nobleman, hence the “von” in his name. He died in Hamburg in 1686.

abschnitte.titel: The invention of the air pump
abschnitte.text: At that time, many scholars, relying on the Greek thinker Aristotle, believed that nature could not tolerate empty space. Guericke wanted to test this and built the first **air pump** around 1650. With it, he pumped air out of containers and created a **vacuum**. He showed that in airless space no candle burns, no sound is carried and animals cannot breathe.

His most famous experiment: two hollow copper hemispheres were put together and the air was pumped out. After that, the **air pressure** from outside pressed the hemispheres together so tightly that teams of horses on both sides could not separate them. When air was let back in, the halves fell apart by themselves. Guericke gave such demonstrations in front of princes, including at the Imperial Diet in Regensburg in 1654.

Guericke also built a rotating **sulphur ball** that became electrically charged when rubbed by hand. It attracted light things such as feathers and is considered one of the first machines for producing electricity. He also noticed that air pressure varies and used this to predict changes in the weather. This made him a pioneer of meteorology.

He described his experiments in a large book in **Latin**, the language of scholars. It was published in Amsterdam in 1672 under the title “Experimenta nova Magdeburgica de vacuo spatio”, roughly “New Magdeburg experiments on empty space”. Today the Otto von Guericke University Magdeburg bears his name. The vacuum technology he founded is found today in light bulbs, vacuum flasks and vacuum packaging.

begriffe.erklaerung: A space in which there is (almost) no air and no other particles.
The force with which the air of the Earth's atmosphere presses on everything.
A device for sucking air out of a container.
A great war in Europe from 1618 to 1648.

gewusst: A well-known picture shows 16 horses, eight on each side, pulling at the hemispheres in vain.
Guericke also built a water barometer more than ten metres high on his house.
In Magdeburg, the hemisphere experiment is still re-enacted at town festivals today.

teile.einleitung: An oscilloscope is a measuring device that makes electrical voltages visible as a curve on a screen. This lets you see how a voltage changes within fractions of a second. For electronics engineers and technicians, it is one of the most important tools.
wichtigste: An oscilloscope shows time horizontally and voltage vertically.
The screen is divided into squares with which you can read off times and voltages.
The trigger makes sure that a repeating signal appears as a still picture.
Classic analogue oscilloscopes produced their image with a cathode ray tube.
Today's digital oscilloscopes sample the signal and store it.
Current is measured indirectly through the voltage across a known resistor.
In XY mode, two oscillations create Lissajous figures.

abschnitte.text: An oscilloscope draws a graph in real time. **Time** runs along the horizontal axis, and **voltage** is shown on the vertical axis. This turns an invisible electrical oscillation into a visible curve. You can see, for example, whether a signal looks like a gentle wave, a square or a zigzag.

The screen has a grid of squares. With the **timebase**, you set how much time one square stands for horizontally, for example 0.5 milliseconds. If one oscillation is 4 squares wide, it lasts 2 milliseconds and the frequency is 500 hertz. The same applies vertically: if a signal reaches 3 squares high at 2 volts per square, the peak value is 6 volts.

Without help, the curve would race across the screen and flicker. The **trigger** always starts the drawing at the same point of the oscillation, for example when the voltage rises above a certain value. This makes all the sweeps lie exactly on top of each other. The result is a still, easy-to-read picture.

In the past, oscilloscopes worked with the **cathode ray tube**, which Karl Ferdinand Braun invented in 1897. In it, the voltage deflected an electron beam that drew a dot on a glowing layer. Today most oscilloscopes are digital. They measure the signal very many times a second and show it on a flat screen, and the sampling rate must be more than twice the highest frequency in the signal.

Oscilloscopes are found in workshops, laboratories and schools, and are used when repairing cars and appliances. As the device only measures voltages, you send a current through a known resistor and measure the voltage across it. In **XY mode**, a second voltage controls the horizontal direction instead of time. This produces pretty loops and curves, the Lissajous figures.

begriffe.erklaerung: The setting for how much time one square on the screen stands for.
A starting signal that makes the curve stand still.
The number of oscillations per second, measured in hertz.
The highest value a voltage reaches in an oscillation.
Loop patterns created by combining two oscillations.

gewusst: For a long time, the cathode ray tube from the oscilloscope was also the picture tube in old televisions.
Good oscilloscopes can show events that last only billionths of a second.
The logo of the Australian broadcaster ABC is a Lissajous figure.

teile.einleitung: Ohm's law describes how voltage, current and resistance are related in an electric circuit. It was formulated in 1826 and 1827 by the German physicist Georg Simon Ohm. With the formula U = R · I, you can answer many questions about electrical appliances.
wichtigste: Ohm's law is U = R · I.
The current is proportional to the voltage and inversely proportional to the resistance.
Georg Simon Ohm formulated the relationship in 1826/1827.
The unit of resistance is the ohm, written Ω.
For an ohmic resistor, the characteristic curve is a straight line through the origin.
For a light bulb, the law does not hold exactly, because the resistance rises with temperature.
Electrical power can be calculated with P = U · I.

abschnitte.text: **Ohm's law** links three quantities: voltage U in volts, current I in amperes and **resistance** R in ohms. It says U = R · I. If you double the voltage, the current doubles too. If the resistance is twice as large, only half as much current flows.

If there is a voltage of 12 V across a resistance of 4 Ω, a current of 3 A flows. A **kettle** that draws a current of 10 A at 230 V has a heating element of 23 Ω. If 2 A flow through a resistance of 50 Ω, **heating power** of 200 W is produced. For this you use P = U · I or P = R · I².

If you plot voltage and current on a graph, you get a **characteristic curve**. For an ohmic resistor, it is a straight line through the origin. For a **light bulb**, it is curved. The filament gets very hot, and as it does, its resistance rises sharply.

**Georg Simon Ohm** lived from 1789 to 1854 and came from Erlangen in Bavaria. He was a teacher and did his experiments with equipment he built himself. In 1826 and 1827 he published the relationship between voltage, current and resistance. At first his work was hardly noticed; later the unit of resistance was named after him.

Electricians and engineers use the law every day. With it, they work out how thick cables must be and which **fuses** are needed. Light-emitting diodes also need a suitable series resistor so that they do not break. With a **multimeter**, you can measure voltage, current and resistance yourself.

begriffe.erklaerung: What drives the current, measured in volts.
How much electricity flows per second, measured in amperes.
How strongly a component slows down the current, measured in ohms.
A graph that shows how current and voltage are related.

gewusst: The symbol for the ohm is the Greek letter omega, Ω.
The human body also has an electrical resistance; it is greater when the skin is dry than when it is wet.
A memory aid for the law is the word URI: U equals R times I.

teile.einleitung: The harmonic series is the ordered sequence of all the partials that sound along with a fundamental. Their frequencies are whole-number multiples of the fundamental. The most important intervals in music, such as the octave, fifth and third, can be derived from it.
wichtigste: The partials of an ideal harmonic series are whole-number multiples of the fundamental frequency.
With a fundamental of 110 hertz, the 3rd partial is 330 hertz.
The 2nd and 3rd partials form a fifth.
The 3rd and 4th partials form a fourth.
The 4th and 5th partials form a major third.
There are two octaves between the 1st and the 4th partial.
The strength of the individual overtones decides the tone colour of an instrument.
Fourier analysis can break a sound down into its sine waves.

abschnitte.text: A note from an instrument is made up of many **partials**. The lowest is the fundamental, and above it lie the overtones. If you arrange them by pitch, you get the **harmonic series**, also called the natural series. With a fundamental of 110 hertz, the partials are 110, 220, 330, 440, 550 hertz and so on.

The gaps between the partials give the familiar **intervals**. From the 1st to the 2nd partial is an octave, in the ratio 2 to 1. The 2nd and 3rd partials form a fifth in the ratio 3 to 2, the 3rd and 4th a fourth. The 4th and 5th partials form a major third, the 5th and 6th a minor third.

If the series starts on low C, it is followed by c, g, c', e' and g'. So the first six partials make a **major chord**. Further up, the gaps get smaller and smaller. Some notes, such as the 7th and 11th partials, do not fit exactly into our modern scale.

The Greek scholar **Pythagoras** is said to have studied the number ratios of intervals with a stretched string, the monochord. If you halve the string, it sounds an octave higher. In the 19th century, Hermann von Helmholtz investigated how overtones shape sound. Before that, the mathematician Joseph Fourier had shown how to break vibrations down into simple parts: **Fourier analysis**.

Brass instruments without valves, such as the alphorn, hunting horn or fanfare trumpet, can only play notes of the harmonic series. Only valves, or a slide as on the trombone, make all notes possible. The **clarinet**, with its almost cylindrical tube, mainly emphasises the odd-numbered partials in its low register, which gives it its typical, slightly hollow sound. A tuner or a music app uses Fourier analysis to show which partials are present and how strong they are.

The harmonic series explains why some notes sound especially harmonious together. With the octave and the fifth, many overtones of the two notes match exactly. Instrument makers use this knowledge to shape the sound of bells, organ pipes and strings. In electronic music, too, sounds are built up from individual **sine tones**.

begriffe.erklaerung: One of the individual tones a sound is made of; the fundamental is the first.
The distance between two notes, for example an octave or a fifth.
An interval in which the upper note has double the frequency.
A calculation method that breaks a sound down into simple sine waves.
A completely pure tone without overtones.

gewusst: Our ears can pick out a fundamental from the overtones even when it is not sounding at all; that is how we hear deep voices even from small mobile phone speakers.
The notes of an alphorn all come from the harmonic series, which is why old alphorn melodies sometimes sound unusual.

teile.einleitung: The mains voltage is the electrical voltage available at our sockets. In Switzerland it is 230 volts alternating voltage, in the USA around 120 volts. It is strong enough to run cookers and kettles, and that is why it is dangerous for people.
wichtigste: In Switzerland, the socket supplies 230 volts of alternating current.
For large appliances such as cookers, the three-phase connection with 400 volts is used.
In the USA, the mains voltage in homes is around 120 volts.
Alternating voltages from about 50 volts upwards are considered dangerous.
From power and voltage you can work out the current: current equals power divided by voltage.
Chargers convert the mains voltage into a small direct voltage.
The label “230 V” on the rating plate tells you which voltage an appliance is built for.

abschnitte.text: **Voltage** is a kind of pressure that drives the electric charges through a cable. It is measured in **volts**, named after the Italian physicist Alessandro Volta. In a Swiss home, the socket carries 230 volts of alternating voltage at 50 hertz. For comparison: a normal battery has only 1.5 volts.

The power grid brings three wires, the so-called phases, into the house. Between one phase and the neutral wire there are 230 volts, which lamps, televisions and vacuum cleaners use. Between two phases there are 400 volts; this is **three-phase current**. Large appliances such as cookers, ovens or heat pumps use this connection.

The power of an appliance is voltage times current. A kettle with 2300 watts at 230 volts therefore needs a current of **10 amperes**. A hairdryer with 1150 watts needs 5 amperes. Fuses switch off the current if too many appliances are on one circuit at the same time and the current becomes too large.

In Europe 230 volts is usual, whereas in the USA, Canada and parts of Japan it is around 120 volts. The plugs are different too; Switzerland has its own three-pin plug, type J. That is why you often need a travel adaptor when travelling. An appliance built only for 120 volts can break at 230 volts.

Mobile phones, laptops and games consoles only need small **direct voltages** of a few volts. A charger or power supply converts the 230 volts from the socket accordingly. The **rating plate** shows which input voltage an appliance is built for. Many chargers today can handle anything between 100 and 240 volts and so work all over the world.

Alternating voltages from about **50 volts** are considered dangerous, and 230 volts can cause a life-threatening electric shock. That is why you must never put objects into sockets or use damaged cables. A **residual current device**, or RCD, switches off the current in a flash if current flows through a person. Electrical appliances do not belong near a bath or washbasin.

begriffe.erklaerung: The unit of electrical voltage.
Voltage whose direction regularly reverses.
Current from three phases, which makes 400 volts available.
A device that converts mains voltage into a smaller voltage.
A safety switch that cuts off the power immediately in an electrical accident.

gewusst: With 230 volts alternating voltage, the voltage actually changes all the time and reaches peaks of around 325 volts.
Switzerland used to have a mains voltage of 220 volts; it was standardised across Europe to 230 volts.
A flat two-pin Europlug also fits into Swiss sockets.

teile.einleitung: An objective lens is the lens system of a camera, telescope or microscope that faces the object being looked at. It gathers the light and forms a sharp image from it. Depending on its design, a lens can show wide landscapes, distant animals or tiny insects.
wichtigste: The objective is the lens or group of lenses that points towards the object being looked at.
The most important property of a lens is its focal length.
A wide-angle lens has a shorter focal length than a standard lens.
With a zoom lens, the focal length can be changed.
A macro lens is used for close-ups of small things such as insects.
A fast lens has a large aperture and lets in a lot of light.
A fisheye lens has an angle of view of about 180 degrees.

abschnitte.text: The word **objective** comes from the Latin “obiectum”, the thing you look at. So the objective is the lens that points towards the **object**. In a telescope or microscope, it forms an intermediate image that you look at through the eyepiece. In a camera, it projects the image directly onto the sensor, or in the past onto the film. A lens usually does not consist of a single lens element, but of several glass lenses one behind the other.

A **converging lens** bends the light rays so that they meet at one point behind the lens. The distance from the lens to this point is called the **focal length** and is given in millimetres. But a single lens produces coloured fringes and blurred edges. That is why several lenses made of different kinds of glass are combined, cancelling out each other's faults. Good lenses therefore often have more than ten elements.

A **wide-angle lens** has a short focal length and shows a large area, such as a whole mountain range. A **telephoto lens** has a long focal length and brings distant things close, for example an ibex on a rock face. A fisheye lens covers an angle of view of about 180 degrees and strongly curves straight lines. With a **zoom lens**, the focal length can be changed, so you can switch from wide to close. With a macro lens, you photograph small things such as insects or flowers from very close up.

A lens has an adjustable opening, the **aperture**. If it is wide open, a lot of light gets in; if it is almost closed, only a little. A lens with a very large opening is called **fast**, and it is good for pictures at dusk. With a wide-open aperture, only a narrow zone is sharp and the background becomes blurred. Photographers like to use this for portraits.

Every smartphone has lenses too, often several with different focal lengths. They are tiny and usually made of plastic lenses. Large objective lenses are found in the **telescopes** of observatories, where they are meant to gather as much light as possible from distant stars. Microscopes usually have several objectives on a turret, so that you can switch between different magnifications. Security cameras, projectors and binoculars also have lenses.

begriffe.erklaerung: The distance between the lens and the point where the light rays meet.
An adjustable opening in the lens that decides how much light gets in.
A lens whose focal length can be changed.
A lens that is thicker in the middle and brings light rays together at one point.

gewusst: Fisheye lenses are called that because fish under water are said to have a similarly wide view upwards.
Some telephoto lenses for sport and wildlife photos are longer than a forearm and weigh several kilograms.
A microscope always needs two lens systems: the objective near the specimen and the eyepiece near the eye.

teile.einleitung: Minergie is a Swiss building standard for buildings that use very little energy and are still comfortable to live and work in. It has existed since 1998. A house with a Minergie certificate is well insulated, has automatic ventilation and uses renewable energy wherever possible.
wichtigste: Minergie is a Swiss label for energy-efficient buildings.
The standard has existed since 1998.
The Minergie association is supported by the federal government, the cantons and businesses.
Very good thermal insulation and comfort ventilation are important.
As well as low energy use, high living comfort is a stated goal.
Minergie-P has especially strict requirements, similar to a passive house.
The ECO addition also pays attention to health and building ecology.

abschnitte.text: Minergie is a voluntary **label**, a quality mark for buildings. A house only gets it if it follows certain rules on energy use and comfort. This applies to new houses and also to renovated old buildings. Schools, offices and hospitals can also be Minergie-certified.

The most important thing is a well-insulated **building envelope**: the walls, roof, floor and windows. Thick layers of insulation and triple-glazed windows keep the warmth inside in winter and the heat outside in summer. This means much less energy is needed for heating. You can think of it as a thick winter coat for the house.

**Comfort ventilation** is typical of Minergie buildings. It constantly brings fresh air into the house and takes stale air out, without anyone having to open the windows. A heat exchanger takes the warmth from the outgoing air and passes it to the cold fresh air. You can still open the windows at any time.

The basic standard is simply called Minergie. **Minergie-P** requires an even better building envelope and is comparable to a passive house. With Minergie-A, the building produces much of its own energy over the year, usually with solar panels on the roof. The **ECO** addition can be combined with any of the standards and requires healthy, environmentally friendly building materials and plenty of daylight.

In the 1990s, experts in Switzerland developed the idea of a simple standard for economical houses. The Minergie association was founded in 1998. Today it is supported jointly by the federal government, the cantons and businesses. There are now tens of thousands of Minergie buildings in Switzerland.

In Switzerland, buildings use a large share of all energy, mainly for heating and hot water. Using less energy protects the climate and saves on heating costs. Many Minergie houses are heated with heat pumps instead of oil or gas. Some cantons support Minergie buildings with grants.

begriffe.erklaerung: Materials that stop heat escaping through walls and the roof.
A system that automatically brings fresh air into the house and takes stale air out.
A device that passes heat from warm outgoing air to cold fresh air.
A house that is so well insulated that it hardly needs any heating.
A quality mark that confirms certain properties.

gewusst: In a Minergie house, the people, lamps and appliances noticeably help to heat it too.
The filters of a comfort ventilation system also keep out many pollen grains, which helps people with hay fever.
Even old houses can get a Minergie certificate after a good renovation.

teile.einleitung: The neutron is a tiny particle that, together with the protons, makes up the nucleus of an atom. It has no electric charge, hence its name, which means something like “the neutral one”. It was discovered in 1932 by the English physicist James Chadwick.
wichtigste: Neutrons sit in the atomic nucleus together with protons.
A neutron has no electric charge.
Its mass is almost the same as that of a proton.
The total number of protons and neutrons is called the mass number.
A free neutron decays on average after just under a quarter of an hour.
A neutron star is an extremely dense remnant of a star made almost entirely of neutrons.
The Paul Scherrer Institute in Aargau uses neutrons to study the inside of materials.

abschnitte.text: All substances are made of atoms, and in the middle of every atom there is a tiny **atomic nucleus**. It consists of positively charged protons and uncharged **neutrons**. A neutron is almost exactly as heavy as a proton, just very slightly heavier. It is itself made of three even smaller particles, the quarks. The most common form of hydrogen is the only atom with no neutron at all in its nucleus.

The number of protons decides which element it is. If you add the protons and neutrons together, you get the **mass number**. Uranium-238, for example, has 92 protons, so its nucleus has 238 minus 92, that is 146 neutrons. Atoms of the same element with different numbers of neutrons are called **isotopes**, such as carbon-12 and carbon-14.

For a long time, only protons and electrons were known. But people wondered why atomic nuclei were heavier than the protons alone could explain. In 1932, the English physicist **James Chadwick** detected the uncharged particle and received the Nobel Prize in Physics for it in 1935. A few years later, researchers discovered that neutrons can split heavy atomic nuclei such as uranium; this is the basis of **nuclear fission** in nuclear power stations.

Inside the atomic nucleus, a neutron is usually stable. Outside a nucleus, however, a free neutron **decays** on average after just under a quarter of an hour into a proton, an electron and another tiny particle. In space there are **neutron stars**, the remains of very large stars that have exploded. They consist almost entirely of neutrons, are only about as big as a city and yet are heavier than our Sun.

Because neutrons have no charge, they go deep into materials and are not deflected by electric forces. That makes them good for looking at the **inside of materials**. The Paul Scherrer Institute in Villigen in the canton of Aargau runs the neutron source **SINQ** for this. Researchers there study, for example, batteries, engine parts, magnets or old works of art without destroying them.

begriffe.erklaerung: The tiny, heavy centre of an atom made of protons and neutrons.
The number of all protons and neutrons in an atomic nucleus.
An atom of an element with a different number of neutrons.
An extremely dense remnant of a star made almost entirely of neutrons.
An even smaller particle that protons and neutrons are made of.

gewusst: A teaspoon of material from a neutron star would weigh billions of tonnes on Earth.
The name neutron comes from the word neutral, because the particle is uncharged.
With neutron beams you can look inside an engine or an old statue without cutting it open.

teile.einleitung: A nutcracker is a tool for breaking open hard nutshells. It works according to the law of the lever: a small force on the handles produces a large force on the nut. The colourful wooden nutcracker figures and the Christmas ballet “The Nutcracker” are also famous.
wichtigste: A nutcracker is a lever that multiplies the force of your hand.
You put a hard nut close to the hinge, where the force is greatest.
The macadamia nut has a particularly hard shell.
Well-known wooden nutcrackers often look like a soldier or a king.
Pyotr Tchaikovsky composed the ballet “The Nutcracker”.
In Switzerland, the walnut is usually called Baumnuss.
In mountain forests, the nutcracker bird cracks Swiss stone pine seeds and hides them as a winter store.

abschnitte.text: A classic nutcracker consists of two handles joined at one end by a **hinge**. The hinge is the pivot of a **lever**. If you press at the long end of the handles, a much larger force is produced close to the hinge. That is why it is much easier to crack a nut with a nutcracker than with your bare hand.

For a lever: effort times effort arm equals load times load arm. If, for example, the distance from your hand to the hinge is five times as large as the distance from the nut to the hinge, five times as much force acts on the nut. That is why you put a hard nut as close to the hinge as possible. Pliers, scissors and wheelbarrows use the same principle.

Hazelnuts and **walnuts**, which in Switzerland are called Baumnüsse, can easily be opened with a simple nutcracker. The **macadamia nut** from Australia has a particularly hard shell and needs special crackers. As well as lever nutcrackers, there are also ones with a screw that presses harder and harder, slowly. Some people also crack walnuts by pressing two nuts against each other in their hand.

The colourful wooden nutcrackers that look like a soldier, king or forester are well known. You put the nut in the figure's mouth and press a lever on its back downwards. The figures from the **Ore Mountains** in Germany, where they have been turned on lathes since the 19th century, are especially famous. Today they are mainly a popular Christmas decoration.

The Russian composer **Pyotr Tchaikovsky** wrote the music for the ballet “The Nutcracker”, which was first performed in Saint Petersburg in 1892. The story is based on a fairy tale by the German writer E. T. A. Hoffmann. A girl is given a nutcracker for Christmas, which comes to life at night and fights the Mouse King. That is why the ballet is mostly performed at Christmas time, including in Swiss theatres.

Animals crack nuts too. The **spotted nutcracker**, a bird of the crow family in Swiss mountain forests, opens the cones of the Swiss stone pine with its strong beak. It hides thousands of stone pine seeds in the ground as a winter store and finds most of them again. New stone pines grow from the forgotten seeds, so the bird helps the mountain forest.

begriffe.erklaerung: A rod that turns around a pivot and can increase forces.
The point a lever moves around; in a nutcracker, the hinge.
The Swiss word for the walnut.
A conifer of the Alps, also called Arve or Zirbe, with edible seeds.

gewusst: In German the bird is called Tannenhäher, but in English it is simply called the nutcracker.
A spotted nutcracker can carry many stone pine seeds at once in a pouch in its throat.
A special instrument plays in the ballet “The Nutcracker”: the celesta, whose notes sound like little bells.

teile.einleitung: The phases of the Moon are the different shapes in which we see the Moon in the sky: from a thin crescent to a half moon to a full moon. The Moon does not really change its shape. Depending on the positions of the Sun, Earth and Moon, we simply see a different part of its lit side.
wichtigste: The Moon is always half lit by the Sun.
Depending on the position, we see a larger or smaller part of this lit half.
It takes about 29.5 days from one new moon to the next.
The main phases are called new moon, first quarter, full moon and last quarter.
If the crescent is lit on the right and looks like a bracket “)”, the Moon is waxing.
There are 12 or 13 full moons in a year.
You can often see the Moon during the day too.

abschnitte.titel: How do the phases of the Moon happen?
abschnitte.text: The Sun always lights up exactly one half of the Moon. As the Moon orbits the Earth, we look at it from changing directions. Sometimes we see a lot of the bright side, sometimes a little, sometimes none. This creates the **phases of the Moon**. People often think that the Earth's shadow covers the Moon, but that is not true; that only happens during a lunar eclipse.

About **29.5 days** pass from one new moon to the next. At new moon, the Moon is between the Earth and the Sun and is invisible. After that, a thin **crescent** appears in the evening, growing day by day until, after about a week, you can see the waxing **half moon**. Around two weeks after new moon it is **full moon**; after that the Moon wanes again to the waning half moon and the next new moon.

In the northern hemisphere, which includes Switzerland, the rule is: if the right side is bright and the crescent looks like a bracket “)”, the Moon is waxing. If the left side is bright, like “(”, it is waning. An old German memory aid says that if you can add one stroke to make a handwritten **a**, the Moon is waning (abnehmen means to wane). In the southern hemisphere, for example in Australia, it is exactly the other way round.

You can often see the Moon during the **day** too, for example the waxing half moon in the afternoon or the waning one in the morning. It looks pale then, because the bright sky outshines it. Only around new moon can you not see it at all, because it is almost in the same direction as the Sun. The full moon, on the other hand, rises at about sunset and sets at about sunrise.

Because the Moon returns so regularly, many peoples based their **calendars** on it. Our word “month” comes from the word moon. The Islamic calendar is still a pure lunar calendar today, and the date of Easter depends on the first full moon in spring. As a lunar month is shorter than most calendar months, there are sometimes two full moons in one month; the second is often called a **blue moon**.

begriffe.erklaerung: The shape in which we see the lit part of the Moon.
The thin, curved shape of the Moon shortly after or before new moon.
The phase in which exactly half of the visible disc of the Moon is bright.
The lit part of the Moon gets bigger from day to day.
A common name for the second full moon in a calendar month.

gewusst: A blue moon is not blue; the name just means that it is a rare event.
A lunar eclipse can only happen at full moon, a solar eclipse only at new moon.
Astronauts on the Moon also see the Earth in phases, just the exact opposite of our phases of the Moon.

teile.einleitung: Nikola Tesla was an inventor and engineer who is famous above all for his work with alternating current. He was born in what is now Croatia and lived in the USA from 1884. Many of his ideas are still found in motors, power stations and electricity grids today.
wichtigste: Nikola Tesla was born in 1856 in Smiljan in what is now Croatia and died in 1943 in New York.
From 1884 he lived and worked in the USA, at first briefly for Thomas Alva Edison.
He developed the induction motor, an electric motor that runs on alternating current.
He sold his patents for the alternating current system to the businessman George Westinghouse.
With his alternating current, a large power station was built at Niagara Falls in 1895.
The Tesla coil produces very high voltages and artificial lightning.
The unit tesla for magnetic flux density is named after him.

abschnitte.text: Nikola Tesla was born on 10 July 1856 in **Smiljan**, a village in what is now Croatia, which then belonged to the Austrian Empire. His parents were Serbs, and his father was a priest. Even as a child he had an excellent memory and could picture machines precisely in his head. He studied engineering in **Graz** and then worked in Budapest and Paris. In Budapest he came up with the idea for a motor with a rotating magnetic field.

In 1884, Tesla emigrated to **New York**. At first he worked for the famous inventor **Thomas Alva Edison**, who backed direct current. But the two quarrelled, and after a short time Tesla went his own way. He developed the **induction motor**, an electric motor that runs on alternating current and is found in many machines today. He sold his patents for the alternating current system to the businessman **George Westinghouse**.

At the end of the 19th century, Edison on one side and Westinghouse and Tesla on the other argued about which kind of current should win. This dispute is called the **war of the currents**. **Alternating current** has the advantage that transformers can easily raise it to high voltages so that it can be carried over long distances. In 1893, Westinghouse lit up the World's Fair in Chicago with alternating current. In 1895, a large hydroelectric power station with Tesla's system started working at **Niagara Falls**, and alternating current won the day.

Tesla invented the **Tesla transformer**, also called the Tesla coil, which produces very high voltages and artificial lightning. In 1898 in New York he demonstrated a **remote-controlled boat**, which seemed like magic at the time. He dreamed of sending electricity through the air without cables. For this he had the Wardenclyffe Tower built on Long Island, but it was never finished because the money ran out. Altogether he received several hundred patents worldwide.

Despite his many inventions, Tesla was poor at the end of his life. He lived a withdrawn life in hotel rooms in New York and liked to feed pigeons. He died on 7 January 1943 at the age of 86. Today he is considered one of the most important pioneers of electrical engineering. Since 1960, the unit of **magnetic flux density** has been called the tesla, and a well-known maker of electric cars also bears his name.

begriffe.erklaerung: Current that constantly changes direction, like the current from a socket.
Current that always flows in the same direction, like the current from a battery.
A device that raises or lowers electrical voltage.
A right that protects an inventor's invention for a certain time.
An electric motor driven by a rotating magnetic field.

gewusst: Tesla spoke several languages and is said to have known whole books by heart.
In Belgrade there is a Nikola Tesla Museum, where his urn is also kept.
At 1.5 to 3 tesla, the magnet in a hospital MRI scanner is tens of thousands of times stronger than the Earth's magnetic field.

teile.einleitung: The gravitational field strength tells you how strongly a celestial body pulls on one kilogram of mass at a particular place. In Switzerland it is about 9.81 newtons per kilogram. On the Moon it is much smaller, which is why astronauts can hop about so easily there.
wichtigste: Gravitational field strength is the weight per kilogram of mass.
It is given the letter g and is stated in newtons per kilogram (N/kg).
The unit N/kg equals m/s², which is why g is also called the acceleration due to gravity.
In Switzerland, the gravitational field strength is about 9.81 N/kg.
It is slightly smaller at the equator than at the poles, and slightly smaller on high mountains than in the valley.
On the Moon it is only about 1.6 N/kg, at the surface of the Sun about 274 N/kg.
Among the planets, Jupiter has the greatest gravitational field strength, and Venus has one similar to the Earth's.

abschnitte.text: Every object is pulled by the Earth; this force is called **weight**. The gravitational field strength tells you how much weight acts on one kilogram of mass. The formula is: weight equals mass times gravitational field strength. So in Switzerland, a child with a mass of 30 kilograms is pulled downwards with about 294 newtons.

The unit newtons per kilogram is exactly the same as metres per second squared. That is why g is also called the **acceleration due to gravity**. Without air resistance, a falling stone gets about 9.81 metres per second faster every second. After one second of free fall, it is therefore travelling at around 35 kilometres per hour.

The Earth is not a perfect sphere but is a little fatter at the equator. There you are further from the centre of the Earth, and the Earth's fast rotation also pushes a little outwards. That is why the gravitational field strength is about 9.78 N/kg at the equator and about 9.83 N/kg at the poles. **Height** plays a part too: on the summit of the Matterhorn, the gravitational field strength is a tiny bit smaller than in Zurich.

abschnitte.titel: Gravitational field strength in the solar system
abschnitte.text: The bigger and heavier a celestial body is, the greater its gravitational field strength usually is. On the **Moon** it is only about 1.6 N/kg, roughly a sixth of the Earth's value. On Mars it is about 3.7 N/kg, and on Venus about 8.9 N/kg, almost as much as on Earth. Jupiter has the greatest value of all the planets at almost 25 N/kg, and at the surface of the Sun it would even be about 274 N/kg.

The gravitational field strength can be measured with a pendulum or with falling experiments. Very precise measuring devices are called **gravimeters**. Geologists use tiny differences in the gravitational field strength to track down dense rocks or hollows underground. For scales in shops and laboratories, the exact gravitational field strength is important so that they measure correctly everywhere.

begriffe.erklaerung: How much matter there is in an object, measured in kilograms. It is the same everywhere.
The force with which a celestial body pulls on an object, measured in newtons.
The unit of force, named after Isaac Newton.
How much faster a falling object gets every second.

gewusst: On the Moon, a child who jumps 30 centimetres high on Earth would get almost two metres high.
Your mass stays the same on all planets; only your weight changes.
An object weighs about half a per cent more at the poles than at the equator.

teile.einleitung: Muscle output tells you how much work a person or animal can do with their muscles per second. Like the power of machines, it is measured in watts. A healthy person can manage about 100 watts over a longer time, as much as a bright old light bulb uses.
wichtigste: Power is work divided by time and is measured in watts.
A healthy person can produce about 100 watts over a longer time.
You only reach your highest power briefly, for example in a sprint.
Muscles have an efficiency of about 25 per cent.
Most of the energy turns into heat, which is why we get warm during sport.
In cycling, riders are compared using watts per kilogram.
A cyclist weighing 70 kg who produces 280 W manages 4 W/kg.

abschnitte.text: In physics, **power** is the work done in a certain time. If you lift something faster, the power is greater, even though the work stays the same. The unit is the **watt**, named after the Scot James Watt. One watt means one joule of work per second.

When you lift a mass, the work is weight times height. An example: 30 squats in 60 seconds, each lifting 40 kg by 0.4 m. With 10 N/kg, each squat gives 160 joules, 4800 joules altogether, and divided by 60 seconds that makes **80 watts**. If you lift a 2 kg dumbbell 0.5 m twenty times in 10 seconds, that is 20 watts.

How much power you can produce depends strongly on how long you keep it up. Over hours, a healthy person manages about **100 watts**, for example when cycling at an easy pace. Well-trained professional cyclists can hold several hundred watts for an hour. In a short **sprint** of a few seconds, top athletes even reach over 1000 watts.

Muscles turn only about a quarter of the energy from food into movement. This **efficiency** of around 25 per cent means that 400 watts of energy use produce about 100 watts of mechanical power. The remaining three quarters become heat. That is why we sweat during sport: the sweat cools the skin as it evaporates.

In cycling, especially uphill, it is not only power that counts but also body weight. That is why power is divided by mass, giving **watts per kilogram**. A cyclist weighing 70 kg who produces 280 watts reaches 4 W/kg. A light rider with the same W/kg is about as fast uphill as a heavy one.

In the past, power was measured in horsepower; one horsepower is around 735 watts. So over time a person produces much less than a horse. A small car, on the other hand, has a power of many thousands of watts. Even so, a person on a bicycle is one of the most efficient means of getting around there is.

begriffe.erklaerung: Work done per unit of time.
The unit of power, one joule per second.
The share of energy that is turned into useful work.
A training machine, for example an exercise bike, that measures power in watts.

gewusst: Anyone who cycles at 100 watts for an hour could in theory keep a light bulb glowing for an hour.
In very short sprints on the cycling track, the best sprinters reach peak power of well over 2000 watts.
A person at rest turns about as much energy into heat as a lamp of around 80 to 100 watts.

teile.einleitung: Moore's law is an observation from computer technology: the number of transistors on a computer chip doubles roughly every two years. It is not a law of nature but a rule of thumb that held true for a surprisingly long time. It is named after Gordon Moore, one of the founders of the company Intel.
wichtigste: Moore's law says that the number of transistors on chips doubles roughly every two years.
Gordon Moore described this development in a famous article in 1965.
It describes exponential growth.
In 10 years, the number of transistors therefore grows by a factor of 32.
Dennard scaling has no longer applied since the mid-2000s.
With very small transistors, quantum effects such as electron tunnelling cause problems.
With “More than Moore”, engineers look for new ways, such as stacked chips or specialised chips.

abschnitte.text: Gordon Moore lived from 1929 to 2023 and was an American chemist. In 1968, together with Robert Noyce, he founded the company **Intel**, which is now one of the largest chip makers in the world. In 1965 he wrote an article predicting how the number of components on chips would develop. At first he assumed it would double every year; in 1975 he corrected this to about two years.

A **transistor** is a tiny electrical switch made of semiconductor material, usually silicon. It can switch current on and off and so represent the zeros and ones of a computer. The more transistors a chip has, the more it can calculate and store at the same time. Modern transistors are so small that you can only see them with an electron microscope.

Doubling means that 1 becomes 2, then 4, 8, 16 and 32. After 10 years of doubling every two years, the number is therefore 32 times as large. This **exponential growth** quickly becomes enormous. The first microprocessor, the Intel 4004 from 1971, had around 2300 transistors; according to the rule there would have been around 2.4 billion in 2011, and that roughly matched real chips.

Thanks to this development, computers became ever faster, smaller and cheaper. A mobile phone today calculates much faster than the largest computers of the 1970s. As of 2026, the largest chips contain more than a hundred billion transistors. Without this progress there would be no smartphones, no fast internet and no artificial intelligence as we know it.

For a long time, smaller transistors did not increase the power use per area; this is called **Dennard scaling**. Since the mid-2000s, this rule no longer applies, because chips would get too hot. That is why the clock speed has hardly risen since then, and several processor cores are built in instead. With structures of only a few nanometres, **quantum effects** also cause problems: electrons tunnel through barrier layers that should actually stop them.

Experts are looking for new ways to make chips more powerful anyway. Chips are stacked on top of each other, specialised chips are built for particular tasks such as artificial intelligence, or many small chips are joined together in one package. This strategy is called **More than Moore**. Research is also going into completely new ideas such as quantum computers.

begriffe.erklaerung: A tiny electrical switch, the basic building block of every computer chip.
Growth in which an amount keeps doubling at equal intervals of time.
A material such as silicon that conducts electricity or not, depending on the conditions.
The main processing chip of a computer.

gewusst: Moore's law is more of a self-fulfilling prophecy, because the chip industry used it as a target for decades.
Modern transistors are thousands of times thinner than a human hair.
The name “Moore's law” was not thought up by Gordon Moore himself; other people later called it that.

teile.einleitung: An overtone is a quieter, higher note that sounds together with the fundamental when an instrument or a voice produces a note. We usually do not hear the overtones separately, but they give every instrument its own tone colour. That is why an A on the flute sounds different from an A on the violin.
wichtigste: Overtones have frequencies that are whole-number multiples of the fundamental.
In acoustics, a sound made of a fundamental and several overtones is called a complex tone.
The mix of overtones decides why the flute and violin sound different.
A tuning fork produces almost a pure tone without overtones.
With a fundamental of 110 hertz, the second overtone is 330 hertz.
Without keys or valves, the alphorn can only play the notes of the harmonic series.
In overtone singing from Tuva and Mongolia, the overtones can be heard as a separate melody.

abschnitte.text: A guitar string does not only vibrate as a whole, but at the same time also in halves, thirds and quarters. The vibration as a whole gives the **fundamental**. The faster partial vibrations give the **overtones**. Their frequencies are double, triple, four times and so on the frequency of the fundamental.

With a fundamental of 110 hertz, the first overtone is at 220 hertz and the second at 330 hertz. Careful: overtones and **partials** are counted differently. The fundamental is the first partial, so the first overtone is the second partial. A pure tone without overtones is rare; a **tuning fork** comes very close to it.

When a flute and a violin play the same note, the fundamental has the same frequency. What is different is the strength of the individual overtones. The flute has only a few weak overtones and sounds soft. The violin has many strong overtones and sounds brighter and richer; this mix is called **tone colour**.

The **alphorn** has neither keys nor valves. So the player can only blow the notes of the harmonic series, that is the fundamental and the overtones. Depending on how tense the lips are, the horn jumps to a higher natural note. The 11th natural note lies between two notes of our scale and sounds a little off; it is called the **alphorn fa**.

In **overtone singing**, known above all from Tuva and Mongolia, you sing a low note and use your mouth and tongue to bring out individual overtones. Then you hear two notes at once: a humming note and a whistling melody above it. On the guitar, you can play overtones as **harmonics**. If you touch the string lightly exactly in the middle and pluck it, a bright note one octave higher sounds.

begriffe.erklaerung: The lowest note of a sound; it decides the pitch.
The particular way an instrument or a voice sounds.
The notes an instrument can play without keys or valves.
A bright note produced by lightly touching a string at a particular point.

gewusst: We recognise voices on the phone mainly thanks to the overtones, which every person mixes a little differently.
In the 19th century, the physicist Hermann von Helmholtz was one of the first to explain how overtones decide tone colour.

teile.einleitung: The newton is the unit in which forces are measured. It is named after the English natural scientist Isaac Newton, who described the laws of motion. On Earth, a 100-gram bar of chocolate is pulled downwards with about 1 newton.
wichtigste: The newton, abbreviated N, is the unit of force.
It is named after Isaac Newton.
1 newton is 1 kg · m/s², the force that speeds up 1 kg by 1 m/s every second.
A mass of 100 grams has a weight of about 1 N on Earth.
Mass is measured in kilograms, weight in newtons.
A child of 40 kg has a weight of about 400 N.
Larger forces are given in kilonewtons or meganewtons.

abschnitte.text: A **newton** is the force that makes an object with a mass of 1 kilogram 1 metre per second faster every second. Written in units, that is 1 N = 1 kg · m/s². The newton belongs to the International System of Units, which is used in science all over the world. Forces are measured, for example, with a **spring balance**.

Isaac Newton lived in England from 1643 to 1727. He described how forces move objects and explained that the same gravity makes an apple fall and steers the Moon around the Earth. His three laws of motion are still the basis of mechanics today. In his honour, the unit of force was named after him.

In everyday life people often say “I weigh 40 kilos”, but the kilogram is the unit of **mass**. The force with which the Earth pulls on an object is its **weight**, and it is measured in newtons. So a child of 40 kg has a weight of about 400 N, not 40 N. A bathroom scale actually measures a force and then converts it into kilograms.

How large the weight is depends on the **gravitational field strength**. In Switzerland it is about 9.81 N/kg; for calculations, 10 N/kg is often used. At the poles it is slightly greater than at the equator, because you are closer to the centre of the Earth there and the Earth's rotation has less effect. On the Moon it is only about 1.6 N/kg, but the mass of an object stays the same everywhere.

For large forces, multiples are used: 1 kilonewton is 1000 N, so 2.5 kN is 2500 N. A meganewton is a million newtons, so 2,000,000 N is 2 MN. A car presses on the road with about 15 kN. The engines of large rockets produce thrust of many meganewtons.

Climbing ropes and karabiners show how many kilonewtons they can withstand. Engineers also calculate in newtons for bridges, cranes and lifts. In sport, people measure how many newtons are used to kick a football or push off for a jump. This makes the invisible quantity of force comparable.

begriffe.erklaerung: Something that can move, slow down or change the shape of an object.
How much matter an object has, measured in kilograms.
The force with which a celestial body pulls on an object.
Tells you how many newtons of weight 1 kg has in a particular place.
A measuring device with a spring that shows forces in newtons.

gewusst: An object that weighs 50 N on Earth still has a mass of 5 kg on the Moon, but only about a sixth of the weight.
Climbing karabiners often show values such as 22 kN, which is the weight of more than two tonnes.
The symbol for the newton is a capital N, because the unit is named after a person.

teile.einleitung: The Millikan experiment is a famous experiment in which the American physicist Robert Millikan determined the smallest electric charge around 1910. To do this, he watched tiny, electrically charged oil droplets between two metal plates. The result showed that electric charge only comes in fixed, smallest portions.
wichtigste: Around 1910, Robert Millikan measured the elementary charge very precisely.
He watched charged oil droplets in an electric field between two plates.
A floating droplet shows that the electric force and the weight are equal.
Oil was chosen because it hardly evaporates, so the mass of the droplets stays the same.
Millikan worked out the radius of the droplets using Stokes' law.
All the charges he measured were whole-number multiples of the elementary charge of about 1.6 · 10^-19 coulombs.
Millikan received the Nobel Prize in Physics in 1923.

abschnitte.text: Robert Andrews Millikan lived from 1868 to 1953 and was a physicist from the USA. He did research at the University of Chicago and later at the California Institute of Technology. His student **Harvey Fletcher** helped him with his famous experiment. Millikan received the **Nobel Prize** in Physics in 1923 for measuring the elementary charge and for work on the photoelectric effect.

An atomiser sprays very fine oil droplets into a small chamber. Some droplets become electrically charged by friction. They pass between two horizontal metal plates, a **parallel-plate capacitor**, which has a voltage across it. Through a microscope you can watch the lit-up droplets, which look like little stars.

A droplet is pulled down by its weight and pushed up by the **electric force**. If you set the voltage exactly right, the droplet floats still in the air. Then the weight equals the electric force, so m · g = q · U / d. An example: a droplet of 4.9 · 10^-15 kg floats at 1500 volts with the plates 5 mm apart, so it carries about 1.6 · 10^-19 coulombs.

The droplets are so small that you cannot weigh them. So Millikan let them sink without any voltage and measured how fast they fell. Using **Stokes' law** about friction in air, he could work out their radius and therefore their mass. The buoyancy in air can often be ignored, because air has a much lower density than oil.

Millikan measured a great many droplets and kept finding similar values. All the charges were whole-number multiples of one smallest charge, the **elementary charge**. Today it is known very precisely: it is about 1.602 · 10^-19 coulombs. An electron carries exactly one such negative charge.

The experiment was important proof that electricity is made up of tiny particles. With the elementary charge, scientists could also calculate the mass of an electron. Since 2019, the value of the elementary charge has been fixed in the International System of Units. The Millikan experiment is still rebuilt at many upper secondary schools today.

begriffe.erklaerung: The smallest electric charge found freely, about 1.6 · 10^-19 coulombs.
The unit of electric charge, named after Charles-Augustin de Coulomb.
Two parallel metal plates with an electric field between them.
A formula for the friction force on a small ball moving through air or a liquid.

gewusst: One coulomb is the charge of around six quintillion electrons.
Millikan watched some droplets for hours by steering them up and down again and again with the voltage.
The droplets in the experiment are so small that you can only see them as glowing dots in a microscope.

teile.einleitung: Newton's laws are three basic rules that describe how forces cause movement. Isaac Newton published them in 1687 in his work Principia. They explain why a ball rolls, a car brakes and a rocket flies.
wichtigste: Isaac Newton formulated the three laws of motion in 1687.
The first law is the law of inertia.
Without a resultant force, an object stays at rest or keeps moving in a straight line at constant speed.
The second law says that force equals mass times acceleration.
The third law is called action equals reaction.
For every force there is an equal opposing force in the opposite direction.
The unit newton equals kg·m/s².

abschnitte.text: **Isaac Newton** lived in England from 1643 to 1727. He was a physicist, mathematician and astronomer. In 1687 he published his main work, **Principia**, in which he described the three laws of motion and the law of gravitation. The unit of force, the newton, is named after him.

The **law of inertia** says that an object stays at rest or keeps moving straight ahead at a constant speed as long as no resultant force acts on it. If a bus suddenly brakes, you tip forwards because your body wants to keep going. That is why **seat belts** are so important. A rolling ball eventually stops because of friction and air resistance.

The second law links force, mass and **acceleration**: F = m · a. To accelerate a 1200 kg car at 2.5 m/s², you need 3000 N. From this comes the unit newton equals kg·m/s². If a force of 50 N acts for 4 seconds on a 10 kg object at rest, it reaches 20 m/s.

The third law is called **action equals reaction**. For every force there is an equal opposing force in the opposite direction. A **rocket** pushes gases out backwards, and they push the rocket forwards. That is why it can accelerate even in the airless vacuum of space.

In a lift, you feel the laws directly. If the lift accelerates upwards at 2 m/s², the floor pushes harder on you. For a person of 70 kg, that is around 827 N instead of about 687 N when standing still. That is why you briefly feel heavier when the lift starts going up.

begriffe.erklaerung: The tendency of an object to keep its state of motion.
How quickly the speed changes.
The sum of all the forces acting on an object.
Newton's famous book of 1687 on motion and gravity.

gewusst: According to a well-known story, a falling apple got Newton thinking about gravity.
Newton's laws were enough to fly people to the Moon in 1969.
At very high speeds close to the speed of light, you need Einstein's theory of relativity instead of Newton.
